subtopic: TRIBUTE TO STAFF FOR PERFORMANCE DURING EXTENDED EMERGENCY DEBATE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion which would cure an omission last night. The motion is seconded by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker). I move:
That this House extends its most grateful thanks to all members of the House of Commons staff, officers at the Table, particularly the Hansard reporters, protective staff and all other staff who performed so unselfishly and willingly during the extended hours of the emergency debate which has been concluded.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO STAFF FOR PERFORMANCE DURING EXTENDED EMERGENCY DEBATE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext: I am sure they all feel that is their duty, but I am sure the House will want to show its appreciation by its applause.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO STAFF FOR PERFORMANCE DURING EXTENDED EMERGENCY DEBATE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, seasonally adjusted, the number of unemployed in April was 1,135,000. Unadjusted, the number would be well over 1.25 million, an increase of 0.6 per cent from March. The new rate is 9.6 per cent, the highest since the depression. Employment in manufacturing reached its lowest level since 1978. There has been a decrease of 23,000. There were 17,000 fewer jobs in transportation, communications and utilities. The number of jobs in primary industries other than agriculture is down 16,000. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis):
That the Prime Minister and Minister of Finance take constructive and drastic measures to get Canadians back to work and to reverse the staggering upward trend in unemployment.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST THAT BUDGET BE WITHDRAWN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. The minister must have been shocked this morning by the stunning increase in the unemployment levels. They have increased a full 40 per cent since April last year. That demonstrates in very real human terms the need for changed policies on the part of the government. People losing their jobs today are being excommunicated from our economic system because very few other people are hiring.
Because so many of the causes for unemployment can be attributed directly to government policies, and since one of the government policies is the minister's budget, would the minister tell this House why he persists in refusing to withdraw that budget when that budget increased taxes and destroyed job-creating investment incentives? It is obvious that government policies are contributing to the very high level of unemployment today.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST THAT BUDGET BE WITHDRAWN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first, the hon. member has suggested that we are shocked at the unemployment figures. I must say that I am greatly disturbed at the new statistics that have been released today. I believe the statistics indicate how deep the recession has become. Last August, if the hon. member recalls, Canada had the lowest unemployment it had experienced in five years. Since August, because of the recession, we have had increasing unemployment.
The hon. member then goes on to say that the reason for all of this is the November budget and that the solution is the withdrawal of the budget.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST THAT BUDGET BE WITHDRAWN
speechtext: That would help.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST THAT BUDGET BE WITHDRAWN
speechtext: That is, of course, an utterly simplistic approach to the nature of the economic problem that we are facing, not only in Canada but throughout the world, because as unemployment rates in Canada are accelerating they are, at the same time, accelerating in every developed country in the world.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST THAT BUDGET BE WITHDRAWN
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST THAT BUDGET BE WITHDRAWN
speechtext: With the exception of Japan.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST THAT BUDGET BE WITHDRAWN
speechtext: Germany and the United Kingdom.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST THAT BUDGET BE WITHDRAWN
speechtext:
This indicates a very deep-seated recession that is gripping not only Canada but every developed country. Therefore, if I thought that withdrawing the budget-and that is the suggestion of the hon. member-would solve the unemployment problem in Canada, West Germany, the United Kingdom and France, I would be the first person to do it, but I

May 7, 1982

believe the hon. member has a very simplistic approach to the economic problems of the country.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-REQUEST THAT BUDGET BE WITHDRAWN
speechtext:
I am going to show to the minister, Madam Speaker, that there are three policy areas that can be changed. I am not saying that one is the sole cause of it, that is the minister's simplistic way of evading the answer. But he knows two studies were released just in the past week which show that the Canadian economy is still going straight down, whereas other economies in the world have turned. That is the fundamental difference between Canada and other countries.
I did have a question for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. I hope he will soon be in the House so that I can ask it.

Madam Speaker, I will address my second supplementary question to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. He knows that many lives are being disrupted by the high level of unemployment today. One of the reasons-again, one of the reasons-is the record outflow of capital from this country. Part of that record outflow of capital is caused by his administration of the Foreign Investment Review Agency which is creating an obstruction to foreign capital coming into Canada. Why is the minister trying to continue to make the Foreign Investment Review Agency an obstruction to investment when that investment can create jobs which are badly needed in this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the premise of the hon. member's question is completely wrong. The agency does not create obstruction to investment which brings jobs to Canada. Its purpose is to achieve a good deal for the investor and the Canadian economy. I am surprised the hon. member is objecting to this when that type of activity is what we need to create jobs. He opposes that.
The continued bluster of the minister does not fool anyone in the country. People know that capital is not coming into Canada and that capital would create jobs here.

Madam Speaker, the third area of government policy I wish to deal with is energy. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources' energy
policy has resulted in rigs leaving the country, a sharp drop in investment activity by the oil industry, the cancellation of the Alsands project, Judy Creek and the Cold Lake project, and a reduction, in a broad way, in an industry which had been extremely healthy prior to his coming into office. Would the minister make some concessions in his policy to encourage drilling activity in the conventional areas of western Canada, and will he be changing the 25 per cent back-in to avoid Hibernia and other frontier projects experiencing the same fate which has just happened to Alsands?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have indicated before that the government is carefully monitoring the state of the oil and gas industry. We have taken note of the substantial reduction in royalties which the government of Alberta granted last month under the agreement of last September, and that the government was analysing the situation to determine whether any further steps were required.
We have made changes since last fall. Indeed, we have indicated a great deal of flexibility. Obviously, we have made some changes in the past and we will make some in the future to take into account the reality.
I want to draw to the attention of the hon. member, however, that drilling activity in 1982 in Alberta, in other western provinces and in the Canada lands will be up significantly compared to last year. Even last year, drilling for oil in Alberta was higher than it was in 1980, which was a record year. Therefore I draw to the attention of the hon. member that what we need is more oil, and activity does take place in that regard. Announcements have already been made of exploration worth several hundreds of millions of dollars in the Canada lands. I expect more will be announced very shortly, indeed.
Do you really believe that?

subsubtopic: PRIORITY SOUGHT FOR CANADIAN PAY-TV USERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Communications. One of the reasons why we have unemployment in Canada is that the government cannot get its act together between the various departments. While the minister is trying to promote cultural industries, the Minister of Finance is removing incentives in his budget. While the minister and the CRTC are trying to promote pay television in Canada, Telesat, which is an agency half owned by the government, is actively selling satellite capacity to the Americans. We now have a situation under Telesat current planning where Canadian Pay-TV users would be forced to wait six to eight months for a second satellite in order to supply American contracts. What assurance does the minister propose to make to ensure that Canadian Pay-TV
May 7, 1982

users will have priority on the Canadian satellite system over the Americans?

subsubtopic: PRIORITY SOUGHT FOR CANADIAN PAY-TV USERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think I am on record as indicating my very strong support for having the Canadian Pay-TV system as soon as possible. As far as the Telesat question is concerned if there is indeed excess capacity it is in the best interests of Telesat and Canada that this excess capacity be sold to enable Telesat to earn revenues from that excess capacity.
Before a final decision is made as to who will have access to those satellite channels, there is a two-step process. First, there must be an indication by the CRTC that it is indeed satisfied that there are sufficient satellite channels available for Canadian purposes; second, that matter must be ratified by the cabinet which, of course, is most interested in seeing that a sufficient number of satellite channels are available for Canadian purposes.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is also directed to the Minister of Communication, who did not give the assurance I sought that Canadian Pay-TV users would have priority access to the satellite system. I would like to refer him to the letter sent by Telesat to some of the Canadian Pay-TV licensees in which Telesat refers to firm, committed contracts to sell Anik-C services to American users.
As I mentioned to the minister in committee, I am particularly concerned about the fact that Anik C-3, which will be launched on the first commercial operation of the shuttle next November, was originally designed and tilted to bring service to northern Canada and parts of mid-Canada, but Telesat is currently planning to tilt the satellite south so that it will service American users, not Canadian users. Since the minister's own senior deputy, his assistant deputy minister, is a member and director of Telesat, how could he allow this state of affairs, and why does he not correct it?

Madam Speaker, I think that what is of prime interest to us is ensuring that Canadians have access to a wide range of TV programming no matter where they live in the country. I think the hon. member would agree with me that the CanCom satellite signals which have been made available to every part of the country, now bringing four additional television signals and very soon six to seven new radio signals, have meant a great deal of progress.
On the subject of my not answering the first part of the hon. member's question relating to Pay-TV entrepreneurs, who are not presently guaranteed access, I should like to say that Telesat would like to have formal guarantees from those Pay-TV companies that they will indeed pick up these signals. However, as I indicated, there is a two-step process to ensure
Oral Questions
that primary and preferential use is given to Canadian companies. The first step is via the CRTC, which has a mandate to examine the over-all requirements of Canadians, and the second step is a final decision by cabinet. So, these contracts between Telesat and U.S. entrepreneurs will not become definitive until this two-part process has been completed.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. This morning he will know that, by official figures, we have one and a quarter million unemployed people. At this time of year, springtime, when more jobs should be available than at other times of the year, when it should be a time of growth, it is a time of decay. it is impossible for us to take independent action, unlike a number of other western nations?
I want to remind the minister of this. He refers to the figures in the United States. By reading StatsCanada Information this morning we find that 754,000 Canadians have given up looking for work and do not appear in today's statistics of the officially unemployed. That boosts the figure virtually up to two million unemployed. On the boards across Canada there is only one job available for every 357 unemployed. What advice does the minister have for the nearly two million people who presently are seeking work? What advice does he have for them?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member stated that other countries apart from the United States have responsibilities as well. I agree 100 per cent with the hon. member, and within our own possibilities we are doing everything possible to ease the burden of unemployment. But with the existence of the current monetary policy in the United States and the very high real interest rates, despite great slack in the economy, despite 10.3 million unemployed, there are limits to what other countries can do.
I believe that France is an example in this case. They attempted to ease their monetary policy, they attempted to ease their fiscal policy, but they had, in my opinion, to backtrack, with the result that the Minister of Finance in France, in the face of the monetary policy existing in the United States, had to raise short-term interest rates over 20 per cent, in order to protect the value of the French franc. So the hon. member is right in saying there are some things we can do. But the key solution at the present time does not rest with France or Canada. The key solution rests with the main economic partner we all have, and that is the United States of America.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: APPLEBAUM-HEBERT COMMISSION RECOMMENDATIONS- OPPORTUNITY FOR RESPONDING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Communications. Last night, in a speech before the Canadian Conference of the Arts, he attempted to lay at rest the fears that some have, that the minister intends to be the architect of cultural policy and not the Applebaum-Hebert Commission. He suggested, Madam Speaker, that one should not be concerned about the fact that there are study groups already working in advance of the recommendations because there would be time at the end of the consultation and input provided one responded quickly.
Would the minister now tell the House and those who want to respond to Applebaum-Hebert, who want to believe in this process, how much time will be allowed after publication of the recommendations? What forum will be available for comment, will it be the parliamentary committee, will it be briefs to the minister, how long, and what method is open to those people who believe deeply that the Applebaum-Hebert process is essential? What forum will they have and how long will they have to make their presentations?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in my speech last night I indicated that, from my

May 7, 1982

point of view, the main role of government in general in the field of arts and culture was to try to establish a climate for creativity. That indeed is the proper role of government in that area, not one of trying to direct or to be involved in the creative arts themselves. I also indicated that we will be looking forward to the report which will be forthcoming shortly, within the next few months, from the Applebaum-Hebert committee. Out of this report, of course, will flow a number of actions on the part of the government. For instance, I think that the report in some cases will give rise to legislation. Obviously, there will be a good deal of time available for debate and to make representations in front of parliamentary committees.
Other matters, 1 suspect, will call upon the government for immediate action in certain areas. Actually, we have taken that immediate action in some areas of immediate concern, like the clarification of the National Gallery position.
What I did indicate to the group last night was that I was not interested in going from one review committee, that is, the Applebaum-Hebert committee, to another forum which would repeat the Applebaum-Hebert process. I encouraged all people interested in the arts in the country to be ready to respond to the report of the Applebaum-Hebert committee as soon as possible after that document is published. I expect that there will be a month or two available to them to respond.

Madam Speaker, if they want to respond they would feel better about responding if they can believe that the decisions as to what the policy will be have not already been taken. Therefore, let me ask this supplementary, Madam Speaker.
With regard to that essential concept of our culture policy, which is the broadcasting policy, last night the minister said that the development of the broadcasting policy will wait on the publication of the Applebaum-Hebert report; and yet to the committee on his estimates, Madam Speaker, he indicated that a broadcasting policy was effectively already finished. Could the minister tell the House, and those who are worried about this issue, and who want to make submissions, which is true?
Will broadcasting policy wait on the Applebaum-Hebert process so that those who want to comment can, or is it a fact, as the minister already suggested in committee, that the policy is already drafted, already ready to go, and that the minister now is simply saying that we are waiting for the Applebaum-Hebert report simply for form's sake?

Madam Speaker, I have never suggested in any forum that all the T's are crossed and all the I's are dotted on the broadcasting policy. I indicated that the department has indeed set up a number of working groups in order to be able to respond to Applebaum-Hebert as quickly as possible. The whole question of copyright is one example. LOSS OF FISHING VESSEL OFF WEST COAST-REASONS FOR ABANDONING SEARCH
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question today is for the Minister of Transport, and it is also on the search and rescue theme. Some time ago a fishing vessel by the name of the Ramsay Isle disappeared off the west coast of British Columbia. On February 28 a search was mounted by the combined forces of the Coast Guard and the Department of National Defence. The search was eventually abandoned on about March 6. Eight weeks later four bodies were found in a lifeboat, and indications were those people may have died of starvation off the north end of Port Hardy. Is the minister able to cast any light on the situation as to why a search was abandoned when people were in fact still in the water in lifeboats?

subtopic: LOSS OF FISHING VESSEL OFF WEST COAST-REASONS FOR ABANDONING SEARCH
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I did indeed look into that case with the same question in mind, and the answer I got was that the search and rescue operation proceeded in the normal way. Six days were spent at it. Debris was found in the water. After a while, not finding any bodies or survivors, the operation ended, as these operations usually do, in due course. A few months later, two or three bodies were found in a raft a good number of miles-I cannot remember how many, but a surprisingly long distance away-from the place where the accident had taken place. This apparently surprised everybody. The coroner is having an inquest into the matter, and I presume we will learn more about what happened.

Madam Speaker, the situation which seems to be developing with respect to search and rescue facilities is incredible, when we consider cases like the Hudson Transport, the Ocean Ranger, and numerous others. An interesting part of search and rescue is the element of communications. The indication from officials of the minister's department is that there was no Mayday sent out in this case. Now other sources indicate that in fact there were two Mayday broadcasts from that vessel. Is it possible for the minister to indicate whether that is the fact, and why is there a discrepancy in terms of the information we have?
No, Madam Speaker, I am not aware of the Mayday aspect of this rescue operation, but I will find out and report.

subsubtopic: DELAY IN LUMP-SUM PAYMENTS TO EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Transport. As the minister knows, November 15, 1981 was the cut-off date for CN and CP employees to sign the special agreement for those affected by the VIA Rail reductions. Within this agreement it says that from November 15, when an employee reaches age 55, he is eligible for a lump-sum payment. Many employees are eligible for this payment. However, there have been delays in CN's and CP's paying out this money. In those cases where payment has been delayed no accrued interest has gone to the employees. CN and CP are saying they refuse to pay this interest because of government policy.
I wonder if the minister would explain to the House and, more particularly, to those employees who have been so adversely affected because of losing this money, what exactly is the rationale in CN's and CP's not paying this interest to their former workers.

subsubtopic: DELAY IN LUMP-SUM PAYMENTS TO EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will try. I thank my hon. friend for reminding the House of the fair way in which the government is treating employees affected by VIA cuts. He is aware that $30 million has been assigned to that purpose, and lump-sum payments are but one of the methods which are being used.
The way it goes is this: an employee receives his lump-sum payment from the railways: if there is a delay in establishing the amount to which he is entitled, it could be at that stage. The railways then make a claim to the Department of Transport, and the Department of Transport pays the sum claimed by the railways. My surveillance of the system has not been such that I know how many days it takes for my department to pay the railways after a claim has been made, but I will find out and, if it is abnormal, I will try to remedy the situation.

subsubtopic: DELAY IN LUMP-SUM PAYMENTS TO EMPLOYEES
speechtext: It is about three and a half months.

In so far as the
Correctional Service of Canada is concerned:
(a) The 138 per cent increase in expenditure for the item other services-contracted personnel services over fiscal year 1978/79 as recorded in Volume II of the 1979/80 Public Accounts of Canada is explained by the following factors:
(1)	The CSC reduced its person-years in fiscal year 1979/80 by 255 over fiscal year 1978/79. Pending decisions on which services were to be reduced or eliminated, temporary help agencies were used when positions became vacant.
(2)	On June 8, 1979, a temporary restraint program and staffing moratorium was announced by the government. The general objective of the staffing moratorium according to Treasury Board guidelines was: "Departments and agencies cease staffing actions for the time being, and attempt to cover off the duties of any vacant positions by internal secondments or rearrangements of duties, or other temporary measures, such as the use of acting pay or contracting with temporary help agencies."
(3)	There were a number of organizational changes. At national headquarters the Offenders Program Branch was formed in October, 1978. There were numerous staffing processes for secretarial positions necessitating the usage of temporary help agencies. Furthermore the Offenders Program Branch was completing the Case Management Manual. (This provides for the co-ordinated management and administration of the inmate's sentence from the commencement date of his sentence to the date of expiry of the sentence imposed by the court.)
The executive secretary's branch was also newly created in 1979/80 and required a relatively high number of staffing actions thus calling for the use of temporary help agencies.
(4)	In the Pacific region the employee turnover for 1979/80 averaged 16 per cent, pending the relocation of the regional headquarters offices in Vancouver to Abbotsford, approximately 12 employees sought and secured employment elsewhere. The region also faced an increase in administrative work because of the closure of British Columbia Penitentiary on May 10, 1980. The prairie region also experienced an increase in turnover rates of support staff particularly in the province of Alberta.

BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-UNEMPLOYMENT Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East) moved:
That this House, caring for the 1,200,000 Canadians now unemployed and the millions more worried about their jobs, recognizes that the National Energy Program and the budgets of October, 1980, and November, 1981, are largely responsible for this massive unemployment, and demands the resignations of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Finance, and the introduction of a new energy policy and a new budget to create jobs, lower interest rates and restore hope and confidence to Canadians.
May 7, 1982

He said: Mr. Speaker, as we commence this debate on this important motion which is a part of our supply procedure and part of the traditional way that Parliament has of holding the government accountable, I note that there is not a single minister present in the House. Not one minister.

["Order, please. Before I call it five o'clock it has been brought to my attention that comments made by the Chair earlier with respect to a point of order raised by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) may have been out of order in that they constituted an opinion. Just so that members will understand, the hon. member for St. John's East rose on a point of order in reference to the quorum call the other evening. I refused to recognize the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith) for the simple reason that sometimes it does appear to be the duty of the Chair to assist the House in avoiding friction. So it would hardly be consistent if in fact by my intervention I were to add to the friction.
I want to indicate that were it indeed a statement of opinion by the Chair, it was completely inadvertent, and I apologize particularly to the hon. member for St. John's East and to members generally. Obviously it was not my intention to fuel any fires but rather to try and calm them down or put them out.
It being 5 p.m., it is my duty to inform the House that pursuant to Standing Order 58(11) proceedings on the motion have expired. Therefore, the House stands adjourned until Monday at two o'clock p.m., pursuant to Standing Order 2(1).
At 5 p.m. the House adjourned, without question put, pursuant to Standing Order.", 'Monday, May 10, 1982']
Just like last night.
Not even the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey) is here.

One would expect that there would be at least one or two ministers who would have some responsibility in the area of economic affairs. But nobody is here. I see the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) entering the chamber now.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: He is the minister of unemployment, the great job creator.

At least now we have one minister here. Whether or not he will get the message remains to be seen. You know, Mr. Speaker, that is really consistent with the attitude of this government. We all listened a few days ago to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) who spoke in this House giving us the Liberal philosophy of government. I will paraphrase what he said: "The challenge of government is to rise above events." Another way of putting that is: "We do not have time to pay any attention to what is going on around us." The Liberals have other things to do. 1 would remind the government and I would remind the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources if he were here, that the people of Canada want a government that is attentive to events and to what is going on around them and one that will do something about the situation.
Today we meet in a Parliament that is nasty and angry. Certainly I have not experienced anything like this Parliament in my 22 years in this House. I notice you are nodding your head as well, Mr. Speaker. There is a mood of nastiness and a mood of anger in this place. That is as it should be because that is a reflection of the mood of anger that is out there in the country. The country is frenzied; the country is angry, and well it should be.
We listened today to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) replying to questions in response to the disastrous unemployment figures released today. He said to blame the problem on everything but his own budget and disastrous policies. This situation today is unprecedented since the great depression. Today in this country one in ten people are officially out of work. Today in this country the percentage of unemployed is in double digits. We have a rate of inflation that is hovering around 12 per cent, almost twice as much as the rate of inflation in the United States. We have an energy policy that is shattered, which will mean increased energy costs for

this country. I will exacerbate the already serious inflationary situation. It will mean increased gasoline prices. It will mean increased home heating oil prices. These increases come from a government that committed itself two years ago to keeping energy prices down.

speechtext: Below 14 cents.

A commitment was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to keep the excise tax on gasoline below 14 cents. Now we have increases in gasoline amounting to 75 cents. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We did not even tax that.

What do hon. members think of this statement?
Your high interest rate policy would slow down the economy: it will mean the loss of thousands of jobs; it will mean increases in the cost of living. It will probably bring the housing and construction industry to a halt, with thousands of jobs being lost in those sectors.
It will put housing beyond the reach of most middle and lower-income Canadians. It will hurt small business, which depends on bank borrowing to operate. It will hurt farmers, who have the same dependency on bank borrowing and will add, therefore, to the cost of food.
How profound! I wish I had said that. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) uttered those words on October 30, 1979 when he was finance critic and was speaking before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. That is the same Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce who made a commitment that if interest rates rose he would resign. He is still sitting in his place and uttering the empty rhetoric to which we have grown accustomed day after day after day.
The situation is desperate, Mr. Speaker. Directly as a consequence of the last two budgets of the Minister of Finance probably the biggest tragedy in this country today, in my opinion, is the plight of the young people of Canada who have no jobs and nowhere to turn.
Today we have a 9.6 per cent unemployment rate which translates itself into one in ten people out of work. Between April and July of this year we will have 650,000 young people between the ages of 15 and 24 looking for jobs. Many of them are students who face the prospect in September of higher tuition fees as a result of the scrapping of the established programs financing fund. They face higher tuition fees and no jobs, which means, of course, that many of them will not be able to go back to school. Many of them will continue to be on our unemployment rolls well into the winter. That is a tragedy of mammoth proportions, Mr. Speaker.
Why can we not do something for these young people? The bad news today is only one of a series that we have had in the last seven days. A couple of days ago the Conference Board of Canada released its findings and its forecast. It reported the following:

The decline in economic activity, which began mid-way through 1981 and is forecast to continue well into this year, represents the most severe setback suffered by Canada's economy since the early 1950s.
In other words, the situation is going to get worse. Can you imagine the situation getting worse? Today we have had an increase representing a 40 per cent rise in unemployment over this time last year.
If that were not enough, just a couple of days ago the housing start figures came out. What did we find there? We found a 40 per cent decline in housing starts over this time last year. That situation will get worse. The seasonally adjusted rate arising from these figures amounts to 142,000 starts. Yet CMHC indicates that from 1981 to 1986 we will need to maintain annual housing starts of 210,000 a year. That was providing the activity for the previous five years was at average norms, but it was well below average norms. Therefore, we will need more than 210,000 housing starts a year for the next five years just to catch up.
I cite these figures because you can directly relate the housing crisis to the problems facing young people. Not only do they not have jobs but if they get married they will have no place to live. What a tragedy for this country.
I mention housing because hon. members know, and the government should know, that it is probably the most labour intensive industry in the country. But no doubt we will hear the government say: "We have just made provision by way of the budget to provide interest free loans of up to $7,500 to build
30.000	rental units in the country." That is not enough. That is not my opinion, it is the opinion of the industry. They urgently need loans over $10,000 in metropolitan Toronto right now and they also need that much in metropolitan Vancouver. The
30.000	can be taken up in the two largest metropolitan areas of the country right now.
We also know that as a result of a decrease in supply and a concomitant increase in demand there will be further increases in the price of housing. The situation is going to get worse. It will get worse before it gets better. Yet the Minister of Finance stands behind that disastrous budget which he brought down in the House last fall.
Let us consider the consumer price index which is the measurement of the cost of living in this country. At this very moment in 1982, the cost of living in this country stands at 11.6 per cent. In the United States the consumer price index stands at 6.8 per cent, which is a substantial decline. How do you measure that performance in the United States against ours? When you talk about the consumer price index, you are talking about bread and butter, food for the table, a roof over your head.
Home heating oil is another commodity which Canadians basically need just to live. When measuring these basic necessities we must compare them to their performance in the United States. Not only is it fair to measure the government's performance against the performance of the United States, but we can also compare it to the performance of the previous government which we hear so much about these days.
Let us consider home heating oil. Under our budget, the annual tax on home heating oil would represent 19 cents a gallon, or $155 a year average. The annual tax on gasoline was equal to 39 cents a gallon, or $228 a year. We provided for an energy tax credit to protect home owners, fishermen and low-income earners. The total tax before that credit was $483. The total after the tax credit was $263.
Let us compare that to the budget of the Minister of Finance. Under his budget, the average annual tax on heating oil is $441 per year as opposed to $155 a year. The average annual tax on gasoline is $349 a year as opposed to $228 a year. The total tax before the energy tax credit is $790 per year. However, since there is no energy tax credit the total increase stays at $790 a year as opposed to $263 a year. Is there any wonder why the rate of inflation in Canada should be at the double digit rate and hovering around 12 per cent? These increases come from a government which campaigned on keeping price increases on gas and oil down. What total, complete and utter misrepresentation.
Where is the minister of energy? He was absent for most of the emergency debate and we obviously will not have the honour of his company today. The Minister of Finance is not in the House, nor is the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres). There is one minister present in the House who presumably will be replying on behalf of the government. We see by the economic forecast that the unemployment situation will get worse. As a result of the third piece of bad news which hit our country a week ago today, we now know that the energy situation will get considerably worse because of the government's energy policy. That energy policy, like the government's economic and fiscal policies, is in shatters. There is nothing left of them.
The government's energy policy was based entirely on the so-called megaprojects. Let us examine the collapse of the Alsands project, which God knows has been examined enough in the House during the past 35 hours of emergency debate- save for one unexpected interruption. The collapse of the Alsands project will mean the loss of 35,000 directly related jobs. Since these figures have to be added to the job loss represented in today's unemployment figures, it means, of course, that the unemployment statistics will be worse next month. The collapse of Alsands means a loss in direct investment of $13 billion. It means an addition of close to $12 billion in crude oil imports from the offshore. The spin-off effects from now until the end of the century would have amounted to over $400 billion.
I stated those figures for the record because we must relate what they mean to the average Canadian. To the average person in this country they mean further increases in the cost of gasoline at the pump. Paradoxically, this occurs at a time when world prices are decreasing. It will mean further increases in the cost of home heating oil-with no shelter of an energy tax credit-at a time when home heating oil prices in other parts of the world, including the United States, are going down. This will be the effect on the average Canadian.
Of course, these costs will filter all the way through the economy. Ultimately, it will mean higher food prices, added transportation costs and added production costs. If that is
May 7, 1982

added to the number of farm bankruptcies and the decline in our capacity to produce food, the result is an economic tragedy in this country of unprecedented proportions. We have seen nothing like it since the great depression. Indeed, there are areas of the country where the world recession is not relevant because those areas are, in fact, in a full scale depression.
There are one and a quarter million people officially unemployed in this country. What is not included in the number, however, is hidden unemployment or what I call the "hopeless unemployed." These are people who live in areas like Cape Breton and Newfoundland who have no prospects for employment in certain areas of that province and region. They are the hidden unemployed. If they are added to the official unemployment figures of today there are over one and a half million people in Canada looking for work but who have no job prospects.
As I have already indicated, the real tragedy is the dilemma faced by the our young people. Their prospects are very depressing. Students have no hope for summer employment and even if they are able to continue their education they face the prospect in September of increased tuition fees as a result of the budget of the Minister of Finance.
Young people who wish to get married must face the likelihood, in most major centres of the country, of zero vacancy rates. They will not even have an apartment to move into and will have to double up with their parents. Young couples who look to the future to achieve the traditional dream of Canadians to own a small part of Canada face the prospect of never owning a home in this country. The chance to own a home for the average Canadian is practically nil right now. What a mess, Mr. Speaker. To paraphrase an old election slogan, "Grit times are hard times".
Hear, hear!

It is about time the people of Canada had some say in this matter, because if they were given the opportunity of having some say, my prediction is that the last vestige of dishonest Liberalism, the last Liberal government extant in this country today, would be wiped off the map of Canada.
Hear, hear!

The great Liberal Party of this country would be on the verge of extinction and would have to look to the game laws of this country for protection, to quote the late Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker.
They have three options open to them, as I see it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Go now, next week, or later.
They have three options open to them, if they were to be honest-

Or tonight, or tomorrow.
Supply
-with this House and with the people of Canada. First of all, the Minister of Finance could-
Quit, resign and leave.

-be honest with himself and admit that the budget was in shatters, was a disaster, and bring in a new budget. I suspect-indeed, we are told-that that will not happen, thus eliminating that option. But I throw it out again as a serious suggestion because we are all anxious to get this economy of ours back on the rails. That is the role of Parliament.
I have a second suggestion, and I throw this one out sincerely. It has been repeated time and again during the last 24 to 48 hours, during the 35 hours of emergency debate. The second suggestion would be for the Minister of Finance to resign.
Hear, hear!
Go, go!

His resignation should be joined by that of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, because if both hon. gentlemen were true to the traditions of the British parliamentary practice, one with a failed budget and one with a failed energy policy, they would have no other choice but to resign.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It should have happened long ago!
Resign!
The third option facing the government would be for all of its members to go.
Hear, hear!

That is probably the best option, and I see the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith) nodding. At least he should learn to count beyond 20 before he says another word in this House. But I throw that suggestion out as a serious option because the people of this country have shown, in poll after poll, that they have lost confidence in this government. They have no confidence in the leadership of the Prime Minister. All one has to do is to go to western Canada, to Saskatchewan or anywhere in this country, and one will find that the people have no confidence in the policies, these dishonest policies, I am sad to say, of the Minister of Finance.
One would expect the minister to have some social conscience, given his Saint Francis Xavier University background in the Coady tradition. Of course, the people have also lost confidence as a result of the disastrous, collapsed policies of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Given all of that, the people of Canada have no confidence in the energy policies, in the monetary and fiscal policies or in the leadership of the Prime Minister and they have said so in poll after poll.

May 7, 1982
Supply
If I can paraphrase one other historic figure, "In the name of God, go" and give the people of Canada a chance to react to what they have done. They cannot continue as a government- to paraphrase the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources- to rise above events, because if they do, events will pass them by and they will be, as a party, forgotten in the process!
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The "minister of unemployment"!

-I think we are all aware that this debate is being conducted at a very serious time in the fortunes of this country. There is no doubt that all of us on both sides of this House are deeply sorrowed by the grief which has been caused to those who are jobless. There is no doubt people on both sides of this House are searching in their minds and in their hearts to find some answers to those problems. The hon. member who just spoke has shown a tinge of self-righteousness in his attempt to portray that he is the only one who can speak for the people of Canada.
Let the people speak for themselves.
He showed a certain degree of pomposity when he said that he will represent their points of view.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You are the expert on pomposity.

There are many people on this side of the House who also feel very deeply about what has happened in the country. They set forth their ideas and points of view, but they do so in a different manner. I ask hon. members of the House to stop and reflect for a moment on what we have just heard. Did we hear one constructive idea?
No!
Yes-resignation of the government.
Did we hear one proposal which would add one person to the job market?
Absolutely none!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, yes-resign!
Did we hear any suggestions with any positive direction or thrust? Oh, no.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, resign!
A new budget!

All we hear from the apostles of doom and gloom on the other side are policies of negativism. Oh, do they like trouble. They wallow in the pool of chaos. They stir the pot and they know that Canadians are mad and fighting. One reason is because the cause is clearly there. There is a group of
people in this House who have a vested interest in doing nothing but churning up a sense of pessimism and fear, rather than looking at what is possible and considering the kind of direction and policy which Canadians as a whole should be following. They have nothing to offer, nothing to say; no solutions, no proposals.
You are not listening!
Nothing they say is constructive. All they say is why does this minister or that minister not resign? That is not what the people of Canada are asking for.
Oh yes, they are!
They are asking for answers which can be put into effect. That is the difference between the two sides of the House. That is the reason we are always over here and they are always over there.
Oh, oh!
Hear, hear!
Over the years, the people of Canada have ultimately seen that they can have confidence in the Liberal Party of Canada, which is prepared to look for answers-
But you have blown it this time.
-tough as they may be, and does not simply churn the pot of trouble in order to conjure up frightened fantasies.
Nonsense!

That is the difference between us. That is why the people of Canada expect far more than they are receiving from hon. members in the opposition. I frankly think the people are getting tired of this constant tirade, the bell ringings and the debates being held. All right, that is fair enough, that is what Parliament is for; but when do we hear from the opposition what it would do instead?
We hear of a budget which is three and a half years old. As Tories always do, they dwell in the past to find their answers. But when Canadians ask them where they stand, what do they get? They get a cacophony of different answers. Hon. members opposite make the Tower of Babel look like the Mormon Tabernacle choir. One hon. member says spend more money while another says spend less money. One says restrain while another says don't restrain. We do not know where they stand on anything. The reason is because they do not know either. They have never known. They do not have a policy or a program. They have nothing to offer this House.
Hot air.

The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) had the audacity to berate this government for the initiatives we were taking. But when we ask where the hon.


May 7, 1982

member and his leader stand on the issues, what do we hear? We do not hear one word or a single proposition.
They do not know.

We are engaging in the debate here because we want to find answers and because we do care. Because the hon. member has obviously ignored the kind of initiatives we are taking, I would like to show him how we care. Through the programs of my own department alone, and it is not the only one, we are presently servicing close to half a million Canadians through programs involving an expenditure of over $1.6 billion. We are servicing over 100,000 Canadians in direct job creation. Concerning new programs we signed our eleven hundredth work-sharing agreement affecting over 50,000 workers in this country.
Rather than having the enlisted co-operation of hon. members opposite to work with industries and workers in their communities to develop those kinds of programs, we get nothing but the apostles of negativism coming back. There is an answer that is of great effect and that in fact is being used in the hon. member's own province. But he walks oblivious to the reality; he is simply going to his witches' brew, trying to conjure up his particular potion of pessimism. Mr. Speaker, I do not think that is necessary any more.
We have put in place a number of programs to try to help the unemployed. Just recently we added some major restrictions on foreign workers coming in, to make sure that Canadians have first chance. We have introduced new programs under the unemployment insurance program, Section 38, which are providing opportunities to join, in co-operation with the provinces, in developing new job initiatives in forestry, mining and tourism. These proposals are coming from his own provincial government, but the hon. member is totally ignorant of and oblivious to it. Because they are not prepared to get down to work and share in it. There are job programs in fisheries in his own province that will provide hundreds of jobs for fishermen who are out of work. Again the hon. member is oblivious to and ignorant of that fact and reality. Mr. Speaker, we are not saying that that will solve the whole problem. Time and time again in this House we have said that it is a problem affecting every country in the world. And that is not passing the buck; it is trying to describe how we must be careful and deliberate in the policies that we put together, along with other countries, to try to find some way out of these very difficult times.
Instead, we have a resolution in front of us that says that all will be well if one minister would resign and if we throw the budget out and all the rest of it. If the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) resigned, would that help the unemployment rate in the United States which is now 9.4, or would it bring down interest rates set by the Federal Reserve Board? Will they say: "Oh well, the Canadian government has taken an initial major step, because the Tory opposition told them to
Supply
do so, so we will bring our interest rates down"? What foolishness, Mr. Speaker! What nonsense, what silliness, we are receiving from the members of the opposition.
If we have to discuss our economic problems in real terms, then let us discuss them. Let us not have this infantile child's play that we hear continually from the members of the opposition, that somehow if only the Minister of Finance would resign, if we would throw out his budget, all would be right in the world. All of a sudden, Mr. Speaker, the sun would shine.
In the United Kingdom there is an unemployment rate of 12 per cent. There is a government there which the member opposite has extolled time and time again, saying that the Prime Minister, Margaret Thatcher, is the epitome of economic widsom. They have an unemployment rate of 12 per cent, yet hon. members opposite say it somehow would solve all our problems here and abroad if our Minister of Finance would resign.
When is the opposition going to be serious, Mr. Speaker? When are they going to treat these problems with the kind of serious thought they deserve and quit playing their game of sandbox politics? It is about time this Parliament got down to a serious discussion of unemployment, because it is a serious issue.
Hear, hear!
It is time they faced up to the kind of policy that we have put forward and which we are prepared to change and alter if we receive any kind of reasonable suggestion from members opposite.
We never do, we never do.

What have we got so far, Mr. Speaker? Nothing of a serious or rational or intelligent nature. All we see is that banging of the shoe on the table and that wild rhetoric. The hon. member for St. John's East should read some economic papers and forget some of the rhetorical outbursts of evangelism. That is not what these times require.
Let us put forward the kind of strategy that we are dealing with; let us have a serious debate. Let us erase the kind of childishness we have been receiving from the first speaker and get down to serious debate. Let us talk about the real issues. Let us talk about the trinity of evil called inflation, interest rates and unemployment. They are interconnected and interdependent; they all affect one another.
We have said time and time again that if this country is to stabilize its economy, if it is to bring about the stimulus of growth, we must deal with the issue of inflation. We cannot deal with one problem in isolation from another. We must come to grips with the fact that as long as we have a high inflation rate we cannot bring our interest rates down, and if we cannot bring our interest rates down we cannot allow the private sector to stimulate the economy. That was the whole thrust of the Minister of Finance's budget. It was to provide fiscal and monetary restraint in this country, to try to get that inflation under control, on a decreasing scale, so that we can bring interest rates down.

May 7, 1982
Supply
We are as deeply concerned, Mr. Speaker, about the impact of high interest rates as anyone in this country, perhaps more, because we deal with it every day, not under the sort of poppycock opposition pressure that we hear three times a week-and then they go off and do the same sort of dance somewhere else. We are deeply concerned about the position. We have a strategy in place to try to bring the inflation rate down. Contrary to the NDP, we have not adopted the so-called Reaganomics to do it, because we have one thing that is different; we have maintained the full range of social programs, of unemployment insurance, to ensure that there is proper support and cushioning for those who are affected by these policies.
Hear, hear!

The member opposite from St. John's East tried to reach out and paint as black a picture as he possibly can, saying we are down in the depths of the great depression. He forgets that the great depression did not have a thing called the Unemployment Insurance Act, which provides up to $210 a week for people who are unemployed. It has provided the best, most effective and most reliable income support of any country in the world.
Hear, hear!

He totally ignores that. The Unemployment Insurance Act is doing what it was designed to do-provide a basic foundation for workers who are unemployed until the economy turns. It is a credit to this country that we have been able to maintain that system and use it effectively.
Not only are we providing income support, but we are also using the unemployment system in a developmental way to provide opportunities for workers who are unemployed to get new training during that period of time, to go back to work in forest management projects, something which is desperately needed in order to improve the productivity of our forest industry. So this government has tried to bring in not just a basic income support, but tried to use it in a creative way.
It is sheer misery!

Ah, now we are hearing the classic shout, that there is sheer misery. I have an interesting proposition to make to the NDP members. Let them ask their own membership, their own workers, if they would like to follow the NDP proposal, which is to let people really become unemployed and not make any money and not go back to work. 1 do not believe in that kind of idea. I believe that Canadians want to work, that they want to be given the opportunity, that they want to be given the chance to work and to make more income. The NDP do not believe in that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) is rising on a point of order.
Would the minister entertain one short question?

I would prefer to hear the question after a short while.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, seeing the member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) rise to his feet, I would only point out to him, when he is looking for answers, that his own community is a major beneficiary of a new program of this government called the Industrial Labour Adjustment Program. It has provided major industrial incentives for new industries to come into his community. It has provided additional subsidies for workers, new training, new mobility. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I have in my office a letter from the mayor of Brantford thanking me and this government for bringing in the ILAP program.
Hear, hear!

We need that kind of moral support at this time, rather than what we hear from the opposition that there is no strategy, that nothing has been done. I suggest to the member for St. John's East that he go and talk to the member for Brant and find out what has been done in his community to provide that alternative for workers in his constituency. Mr. Speaker, we have those programs in place.
We have also brought into place under the budget, Mr. Speaker, an economic development strategy which appears as a direction to develop the economy now and in the future and to provide jobs. We have heard time and time again about the failure of the megaprojects. Mr. Speaker, yes, the pipeline is postponed and the Alsands project is stopped. Did that really have something to do with the National Energy Program, or was it the international oil economy? If the hon. member for St. John's East used any logic at all, he would realize that the United States did not stop all its oil-shale projects because of the Canadian National Energy Program. The Americans stopped them for the same reason the major multinationals stopped Alsands. The reason was they could not get the price for oil they thought was necessary to develop the projects. That is why many alternative energy projects are being stopped around the world.
However, at the same time there are all kinds of other projects going on. We have the northeast coal project providing jobs for over 5,000 people and the expenditure of $1 billion. How did that project get started? It was started through an investment by this government. The Trans Quebec and Maritime Pipeline project employs close to 11,000 people at an expenditure of $800 million. Why are 11,000 people going to work? They are going to work because of an investment by this government.
In the major projects task force report there are 440 megaprojects which were measured by business, labour and government as being prospective during the next two decades. There have been two failures. All of a sudden hon. members opposite say the megaprojects are no more. There are tens of dozens of projects continuing.
Let me talk about the role the opposition plays in job creation in this country. Let me talk about the position taken
May 7, 1982

by the Conservative Party and the NDP on perhaps the single most critical investment in Canada in terms of its future growth, the modernization of our transportation system. It was quite clear that the growth in western Canada in terms of new export markets for potash, grain, sulphur and coal could not go ahead unless we had a new railway system. We had reached full capacity. The railways said they were not prepared to invest the tens of billions of dollars necessary to bring that project about when they were losing $600 million a year because they were not getting anywhere near a fair price for their service. It was quite clear that that project was the key which would unlock a number of new projects in processing, manufacturing and refining in western Canada and also create jobs in connection with new locomotives in London, steel rails in Sydney and railways cars in Montreal. These have an effect right across Canada. However, someone had to take a tough decision to bring the parties to the table and get them negotiating and showing good faith so that a $13 billion investment could be made to create tens of thousands of jobs across Canada. What was the position of the opposition? What has been the position of the Conservative Party and the New Democratic Party, those great prophets of "What can we do?" They are totally against it.
Who pays the bill?

Since we are talking about who is for this and who is against it and about who is interested in creating growth and jobs in the country, 1 ask hon. members opposite to declare in this debate today their commitment to supporting the policy put forward by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), to supporting those negotiations and to ending the kind of foolish nonsense the allies of the NDP-the NFU and the Manitoba farm and labour federations-get into because they oppose progress, development and growth. They are living in the past. We ask hon. members to renounce that today and agree this is an important investment in the future of Canada which will create jobs for tens of thousands of Canadians.
Let Parliament today in a unified form-both sides of the House-support a policy which will provide major expansion across Canada. Do hon. members opposite have the courage to do that? Does the hon. member for St. John's East? Is he prepared to get his caucus to support a major megaproject so that we can bring that kind of growth on? The hon. member pleaded. He wanted something to happen. The Minister of Transport has put something on the table, but the biggest obstacle to that is the kind of political opposition we get from the Tories and the NDP, who are simply paying off their old debts by living in the past. We want to know when they are prepared to get behind major expansion projects and major growth projects. We want to know when they are prepared to begin co-operating during these difficult times and start creating jobs in this country, rather than simply coming forward on a platform of pessimism.
The hon. member for St. John's East says the Liberals are dishonest. I suggest there may be some reason not to trust his comments as well. There may be some reason to suggest there was a tinge of hypocrisy in the remarks of the hon. member for
Supply
St. John's East, because if he really believed in what he said, rather than standing here berating us he would be working in his own caucus to get agreement and co-operation from his colleagues for something which will provide tens of thousands of jobs in the next year. There will not just be direct jobs in construction and manufacturing; there will also be an opportunity to open up a whole new export market. The hon. member for St. John's East wants a response. That is fair. Should he resign if he is not prepared to co-operate? Should we ask for his resignation because he is dishonest and hypocritical in not being prepared to take the kind of initiative on behalf of the people of Canada that is necessary?
In addition to that, in terms of an economic development strategy we have also put forward a number of initiatives in the area of science and technology in manufacturing. There has been a 20 per cent increase in funding for the National Science and Energy Research Councils for new manufacturing development. Seventy million dollars is going into new centres for microelectronics to aid and assist that fast-growing industry. Millions of dollars are going into the Telidon project, which is providing jobs in the high tech area. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is working on an agri-food strategy, which will provide major support for research in agricultural processing and development. A major study is going on in the fisheries industry to provide for realignment and rationalization with respect to production.
In talking about the economy, let us talk about the statistics which came out yesterday. The hon. member for St. John's East was very anxious to pick and cull from the newspapers all the bad news he could find. Why did he not refer to the good news, which is that we have made the biggest sale of wheat to China in the history of Canada? It was announced yesterday that we have the largest trade surplus ever recorded in this country. That trade surplus is because of a major increase in the export of finished goods. Thirteen billion dollars in the first three months of 1982 is not a bad record. It is exports that will get this country into a better economic position, as long as we can take care of the other problems and as long as we can stay competitive economically and internationally. That means we have to be talking about wages, prices and investment. We have to get the inflation rate down if we are going to maintain our economic advantage.
My contention is that we have a strategy. It was put forward in the budget, both in terms of fiscal and monetary instruments. We have a strategy which relates to a major retraining of Canadians. Hon. members want to talk about productivity and future progress. We increased the training budget of this government by 15 per cent, to over a billion dollars. This will provide training for close to 275,000 Canadians. Hon. members talk about yong people. The best opportunity for a young person is to get the skills he or she will need for the jobs of the future. That is what this government is investing in, with absolutely no help from hon. members opposite.
1 will put another proposition to the hon. member for St. John's East, who is so anxious to get things going. Let him go

back to his caucus and ask if they will agree to a one-day debate on our national training policy so that we can get it through and get the job of training hundreds of thousands of Canadians done. The problem is that the opposition holds up measures like the new national training program which we have not been able to bring forward.
