speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It being one o'clock, I do now leave the chair until two o'clock this afternoon.
At one o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2.00 p.m.
["It being one o'clock, I do now leave the chair until two o'clock this afternoon.\nAt one o'clock the House took recess."]

Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome the opportunity to lead off for my party this afternoon in the debate on the motion proposed by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath).
Before I begin I should like to say that even though I have a great deal of respect for the hon. member in whose name the motion appears, as I sat listening for 30 minutes this morning trying to find a Conservative alternative in his speech regarding an energy strategy or an employment strategy or an industrial strategy, I was disappointed.
I am afraid this is the story of the Conservatives in opposition these days. They want to bash the government, as we do, and they want to be extremely critical. Unfortunately, however, they are critical in a negative way day after day. They do not offer any positive, alternative proposal. That is the major problem with that party. We are not getting a positive response from the Conservatives. I strongly suspect the reason for this is that their leader and their spokesperson on finance have agreed that high interest rates are the only way to bring down
inflation. And that is the government's policy. The critic of the Progressive Conservative Party on finance has stated openly outside this House that he agrees with supply side monetarist Reaganomics. In that way they have preempted themselves from any positive alternatives to any Liberal program or nonprogram at this time.
I was also shocked when the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) intervened before lunchtime and said at the beginning of his speech, and I wrote his words down, "We are all saddened by the grief that is caused to those who are jobless."
I honestly do not understand how the minister who is chiefly responsible for employment, and indeed unemployment in this country, can be so callous in his opening remarks on such serious matters as employment, an industrial strategy and an energy strategy.
In the past few days we have seen the almost total collapse of the major economic thrust of the government, that is, the resource-based capital intensive megaprojects. They have not all gone but certainly the cornerstone has gone. We anticipate that many other megaprojects are not only in jeopardy but may fail as well.
The main reason for this is high interest rates and lower world prices for oil caused by a world glut which the government should have seen and addressed well over a year ago. There is no excuse for putting all the economic eggs in one basket which all of a sudden has a huge hole in it. This has only added to the misery of the 1.2 million Canadians, 9.6 per cent of the work force, who today find themselves jobless. It is a very sad state of affairs.
What makes it tragic is that this recession is a planned recession. It has not come about as a result of normal market forces. The marketplace has not caused this recession. It has come about, first of all, because government has deliberately planned and executed a policy of high interest rates, cuts in public services, cuts for wealthy corporations and wealthy individuals, which in turn have led to massive lay-offs, plant shutdowns and demands for wage rollbacks.
I think it is absolutely unforgivable that government policy today should pit one worker against another; they are bidding each other down to get the lowest paying job in order to keep their heads above water. That is what their fathers had to do during the great depression of the 1930s. Today in many communities across the country we find workers bidding against each other and losing many of the benefits of collective agreements arrived at through negotiation in the sixties and seventies, only to end up competing with each other in a job that pays them less at the end of every week.
As far as I am concerned, that is totally inexcusable. Canada and this government is on a crusade against inflation where jobs are mere cannon fodder. Workers' economic security is the number one casualty. Workers are blamed for inflation- the worker's belt must be tightened, the Prime Minister (Mr. May 7, 1982

Trudeau) has said. In the last five and a half years the wages of workers have fallen behind and today the average worker is $39.19 per week behind where he was in 1976. Yet the Prime Minister says public sector employees, and by implication private sector employees, must tighten their belts for his errors and the errors of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). That is the way it has always been with the Liberals, and it is absolutely despicable as far as I am concerned.
Wages do not cause industrial lay-offs. Just two weeks ago about 4,000 chief executive officers across Canada were polled, and 75 per cent of them said it was not labour unit costs which were causing lay-offs or shutdowns, it was high interest rates and the cost of borrowing money. So it is a planned recession, Mr. Speaker.
I would like to present our option; unlike the Conservatives, we have one. We are not saying it is perfect or will put Canadians back to work in a few days, but at least we have given it thought for several months, analysed it, and we think in the long term it will work. But, like all long-term policies, we have to begin yesterday.
We just cannot afford to drift any further into economic chaos and social distress. The NDP economic strategy is based on a number of key elements, including a historic commitment to Canadianization of our economy through the use of all the tools at our disposal-public enterprise, joint public-private ventures, co-operative ownership and private ownership. Second, the widening of public ownership in the resource sectors; and third, a commitment to require multinational corporations in Canada to provide jobs here which match the level of their access to our markets.
The first two elements are well-known and need no specific elaboration here. The third requires some expansion because it has received attention in recent discussions of our new employment option.
The insistence that multinationals not have free access to our market is of crucial importance in a period of deep recession. This is especially true in the hard-hit manufacturing sector where 308,000 jobs have been lost in the last six months. The weakness of employment in the manufacturing sector is far more severe than it has to be in relation to the size of our market. In 1981 our trade and manufacturing deficit reached a record $21 billion. That deficit cost us 200,000 production jobs and tens of thousands more in the service sector. Even though Statistics Canada has, to date, failed to produce figures on exactly how much of the manufacturing deficit has been caused by multinationals, other studies tell us it is a very high proportion. Foreign-owned corporations account for 57 per cent of Canadian manufacturing. Those firms are concerned first and foremost with their global balance sheets, not with their contribution to Canadian economic wellbeing. Such firms have a marked tendency to import technology, production machinery, parts and components from their head offices. Especially since the recent GATT agreement has lowered
Supply
tariff protection to very low levels, multinational manufacturing firms have had a tendency to shift their production out of Canada to plants in their country of origin.
Without fully understanding it we are now involved in a life or death war of non-tariff barriers to protect our manufacturing employment. Our competitors in the United States, Japan and western Europe are using government policies to maximize their domestic employment. Alone among the major industrialized nations of the world Canada has failed to take serious steps to do this. It is disgusting, embarrassing, and it is Liberal policy. The result is de-industrialization. That does not refer to the temporary loss of jobs in manufacturing as a result of recession; it refers to the shifting of jobs out of Canada by multinationals to their country of origin while the multinational retains or even increases its market share in Canada. Deindustrialization reduces our industries to warehouse-assembly operations. It threatens our very survival as an individual and independent industrial nation. Let me cite the results of two of the studies which confirm this analysis.
A study of U.S. multinational corporations produced by the U.S. Senate in February, 1973, detailed the behaviour of U.S. firms abroad. The study examined the trends in employment and manufacturing in U.S.-owned multinational corporations in seven countries: Canada, the United Kingdom, Belgium-Luxembourg, France, West Germany, Mexico and Brazil. Between 1966 and 1970 U.S. multinationals increased their share of manufacturing employment in those seven countries by an average of 25 per cent. The only country in which there was a decrease in the proportion of manufacturing workers employed by U.S. multinationals was Canada. This decrease was not an indication of lessening U.S. control of our economy; it occurred at the same time as they increased their share of manufactured goods sold in the Canadian market.
Evaluating the evidence, Mr. Speaker, the Senate study concluded that U.S. multinationals had a marked negative impact on Canadian manufacturing employment between 1966 and 1970, the reverse of the pattern in every other country. U.S. firms, while increasing their dominance of the market, were cutting back their relative share of employment. This can best be explained by the growing tendency of U.S. firms to import parts and components manufactured by their U.S. operations into Canadian branch plants for final assembly and sale.
The fact that U.S. manufacturing firms displace jobs in the long run was acknowledged in the study, which concluded that a key role of U.S. multinationals has been to foster the sale of parts and components manufactured in the U.S. to branch plants abroad. We are reaping the whirlwind of that U.S. policy which has resulted in massive lay-offs in many foreign-owned or U.S. branch plants across Canada.
The study estimated, Mr. Speaker, that this role far outweighed the importance of imports to the U.S. from foreign operations of U.S. multinationals. The net gain to the U.S. was placed at 500,000 jobs. Although the study did not break down this job figure in terms of the countries negatively affected, Canada most certainly topped the list. This is so because

May 7, 1982
Supply
Canada is the site of about 25 per cent of all direct U.S. investment abroad. It is further evidenced in light of this study's conclusion that Canada was the only country in which relative employment in U.S. multinational manufacturing firms was dropping.
The second study examined the behaviour of U.S. and Canadian-owned firms in manufacturing in Ontario for the period 1966 to 1972. It concluded that over that period U.S. establishments created only one-third as many new jobs as Canadian-owned firms relative to their size. It was again clear that the reason for the difference in performance was not a shift in market control to Canadian firms; rather it was the tendency of American firms to pass on the bulk of their increased activity in Canada to their American plants. The phenomenal growth in our trade deficit in manufactured products from S2.5 billion to $21 billion in just over a decade is the result.
Our long-term answer to this problem must be to Canadian-ize the manufacturing sector. In the middle range, however, we must recognize that multinationals will play a key role in our manufacturing for years to come. At a time when the bottom has fallen out of our manufacturing economy it would be economic nonsense to advocate a sudden shift from foreign to Canadian ownership of manufacturing.
If, then, the multinationals will be with us for some time to come, we have to get tough with them. We cannot allow them to dominate our market without paying for it by providing us with our fair share of jobs. In the NDP's new employment option, we have argued that Canada must insist that foreign manufacturing firms in the transportation equipment and machinery sectors, both massively foreign owned, must produce in Canada as much in value as Canadians consume of their products. They can do this by producing for both our domestic market and our export market, and by purchasing parts and components from Canadian suppliers. But they can no longer cause a huge trade deficit and cost Canadians tens of thousands of jobs as they are presently doing.
There are three possible situations with respect to manufacturing and multinationals in Canada. First, a situation in which foreign firms dominate the market and supply it from production facilities in their countries of origin. This is the situation in the Third World. It is characterized by massive trade deficits and high unemployment. Second, a situation in which foreign firms are required to produce as much in value in the host country as citizens in that country consume of their products. Third, a situation in which industry is owned and controlled by the citizens of the country in which it is located.
Clearly situation three is preferable to situations one and two. This option must be the long-term goal. In the present circumstances, however, Canada is located-and this is a shameful situation-somewhere between situation one and situation two for 60 per cent of our manufacturing, and we are sliding in the wrong direction.
While advocating growth in the share of our market that is satisfied through domestically-owned firms, we must also hold the multinationals to the provision of our fair share of jobs for the proportion of the market which they enjoy. I would like to say that in our judgment this is a workable option and alternative. In this debate today we have put forward a positive alternative to the government. I hope that some day the Conservatives will put their brains together and also come up with some kind of positive alternative.
At least we have some brains.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to participate in this debate on the motion put forward by my colleague and good friend from St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). His motion is a very timely one. It brings attention to the unemployment situation in this country, the massive lay-offs and the high interest rate problems. The unemployment statistics shattered everyone when we received news of them upon waking up this morning, having left the House at around 2.30 a.m.
I hope my friend, the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn), will stay in the House to hear what I have to say because I, too, have some proposals to put before the House to help the conditions Canada is facing today.
I would like to thank the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae) for his courtesy in allowing me to speak out of turn because I have another commitment.
Before I get into the positive end of things, I want to take a look at what is happening in Canada today and speak about the problems as I see them. Two of the major problems we have can be summed up very simply. Canada has a Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and a Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) who are stubborn and have an unbending attitude toward the business community and the energy industry.
Let me put an example before the House. The Minister of Finance likes to say that he has been discussing his budget with the business community and that the business community is in favour of what he is doing. However, let me read from an article in the latest edition of Maclean's magazine dated May 10, 1982:
To add to the Liberals' dilemma, the November budget is still sending shock waves through an edgy business community. Although MacEachen crisscrossed the nation last month to hold private talks with business leaders, participants report that he still refused to admit that his tax change proposals are riddled with major flaws. Businessmen were forced to devote the major portion of most meetings to arguments about the budget. MacEachen, in turn, reacted to the criticism with obstinate fury, apparently convinced that businessmen are deliberately plotting against him.
I met with representatives of the business community as recently as yesterday at noon. They reported that they are not supporting the actions of the Minister of Finance. I see the minister's parliamentary secretary shaking his head, negatively as usual. The business leaders reported that the Minister of Finance is not doing the right thing. They have made concrete proposals to the government, but instead of accepting them, co-operating and sitting down with Canada's business leaders,
May 7, 1982

the minister is fighting them. He is fighting the labour movement as well. In effect he is saying: "I am right; I am not going to co-operate with you". That is what is happening.
Business leaders in Canada are depressed. They are trying to make things work. They are trying to provide jobs. They are trying to create wealth for the people of Canada. But every time they turn around, they are slapped in the face by the Minister of Finance.
There are some startling statistics before us which this government cannot deny. For instance, 12 out of every 100 small businesses went bankrupt in the last four months. That is a terrible situation. Sixty-two per cent of businesses surveyed who are members of the Chamber of Commerce are putting their venture capital outside the country because they do not trust this government. They do not know what next will be changed. They cannot plan from one month to the next, let alone from one year to the next. These are the problems causing this massive unemployment that we see today. It is the uncertainty that people see and because of that the business community just cannot invest.
Next we have the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. What a classic! He has great political power in Quebec. No one gets a nomination and no one can run for the Liberal Party unless he says so. Once I knew about that, I understood why all the members from the province of Quebec who sit in the back rows sit there and bow to him every time he comes into the House. They do not dare stand up and speak against him. I am surprised the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Hudecki) does not stand up and blast the minister of energy.
He is one of the mufflers.

Think about the number of jobs that have been lost at Stelco as a result of the minister's bumbling in the energy field in Canada. The hon. member for Hamilton West should be up on his feet condemning the minister because jobs have been lost in Hamilton as a result of what the minister of energy has been doing.
What about SYSCO?

On television the other night we saw the minister of energy visiting Texas. He was striding along the streets of Houston looking at the tall buildings. He had meetings with oilmen. Do you know what he said to them, Mr. Speaker? He was saying "Come up to Canada and invest. We want your money. We want you to invest your money in the energy field in Canada." But do you know what he says in the House to Canadians watching him on national television? He says "We are going to Canadianize the industry". I say to the minister that he cannot have it both ways. This is a typical double standard.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Give us an alternative.

Just hang in there and I will.
I come next to a speech given by William P. Wilder to the Harvard Business School Canadian Conference. His topic was

politics, oil and economics in the early 1980s. In part his address reads:
The incredible fact is that Canada has faithfully promised the other members of the International Energy Agency that it will put its energy house in order and move to reduce its demand for imported crude oil.
We have done that-7 per cent.

You have done that? But the numbers are increasing, Mr. Speaker. The numbers of imported barrels will continue to increase. I see the former minister of employment and immigration across the way. He is over there saying, "Thank goodness the Prime Minister booted me out of cabinet; I would not want to be in that hot seat now."
He did not boot me out; he did not take me in.
I made a statement the other day in committee that I wish he were back in that particular portfolio.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I know the hon. member would not intentionally, or in any other way, mislead the House. I was not booted out of cabinet; I was not asked back in.

That is a point well taken. 1 thank the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) for drawing that to my attention.
We could talk about the negatives for a very long period of time. I do not think there is any question that the ragtag bunch who are running the country has given us enough ammunition that an individual member could speak for hours in the House on the damage they have done to Canada. But let us talk about some positive things. The very first thing we would do if we were in government would be to withdraw the budget of the Minister of Finance. That would be the very first and the most positive thing which could be done in the country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: What perks did you lose?

I did not lose any. I have been asked by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. Fisher) what perks I lost. I did not lose any perks; I did not have any perks to lose. The parliamentary secretary should know better; I have absolutely no perks at all which the budget affects.
If we were in government there would be at least four major changes in economic direction. First, we would reward the rist-takers and encourage investment. That would be the minimum first step, because awarding risk-taking and encouraging investment is the only way to create permanent jobs in Canada. Most of the tax incentives in the system should remain, because if they go the investors go. We have seen it happen. The statistics show the outpouring of capital from the country and jobs are lost to Canadians; we have seen that as well. I am not saying that there is not abuse in the system because there

is abuse in any system. That must be eliminated. But incentive must remain as a central part of the Canadian tax system and it is not provided in the budget.
Second, we would help the worst victims of high interest rates. The government took the Small Business Development Bond, which was for farmers and small businessmen, and gutted and destroyed it. They said, "If you are going bankrupt, if you are in financial difficulties, or if you are going down the tube, we will lend you money." They do not bother to help the productive small businessman who is hanging in there, creating jobs and trying to get ahead. He cannot obtain any help at all.
Our mortgage property tax credit would have been helping people to the tune of $125 per month right now, which would have effectively reduced interest rates by about 3.5 per cent to 4 per cent. Our energy tax credit program would have been helping those people who are not making much more than the average family income overcome the high energy costs which exist. Such programs are possible if the national government cares about keeping alive Canadians who want to work and build a stake in Canada.
Third, we would apply restraint with the same vigour we did when we were in government. Heaven knows this must happen; it just has to happen. We cannot have three cabinet ministers flying in formation to Winnipeg in their jets. We cannot have a courier bringing a newspaper from Quebec to the tune of $40 when we can walk down to the Chateau Laurier to pick it up. These kinds of abuse must stop.
I could give example after example. Advocacy advertising must stop. They should quit blowing their own horn. I do not mind them informing Canadians of their programs, not at all, but they should quit blowing their own horn with fancy billboards which do not say a thing. They do not contain any information; they do not inform the public whatsoever.
We would give highest priority to getting on with energy projects which guarantee self-sufficiency. I worry when I see the government and the private sector, because the Minister of Finance does not give any kind of encouragement to the business community, backing off these projects. We have an oil glut; everyone talks about the great glut and the fact that we can obtain cheaper oil and everything else. With the way things are in the Middle East, and with the way the government before us made a commitment to the major trading partners that it would develop our resources and let those who did not have them use resources available elsewhere-and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made that commitment in 1978 to the world; of course he has been known to break commitments now and then-I am fearful when we do not develop what we have in the country. One day we could be right back in the same position we were in in 1975, that is, buying imported oil while ours is sitting here. When we do that, we fool the people in the gallery and young people who need jobs when they finish school. We are fooling them if we say that we will go to Saudi Arabia, Venezuela and Mexico to purchase oil because it is cheap. This creates jobs only in those countries, and that is what is being done today.
Also our party would ensure that the automobile industry, both assemblers and autoparts manufacturers, becomes healthy again. We must encourage those who wish to sell in Canada to have Canadian content in those projects, and we must encourage investment in the automobile industry. I am sure the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton would not object to a Toyota or Honda plant in Sarnia. I would not object to one in Brampton as long as it provided Canadians jobs and improved Canadian productivity.
Another thing which should happen is that tax system changes should be announced and public input should be allowed before the changes are implemented. This must happen in the country, and we are committed to doing it. If we were in government, a commitment on economic initiatives would be made with business for a set period of time so that uncertainties will not exist as they do today. The Minister of Finance changes the rules of the game almost monthly. How in heaven's name can business operate without knowing what is coming down the road? The country was built by people who took risks. It was helped to grow by national governments which encouraged individuals that to build was the way to make the nation grow. We must return to that system, and the sooner the better.
Our party is committed to a national recovery program. We are not only committed, we will do it, and we challenge the government to listen to the people of Canada calling for an election. They want one and they want one desperately. 1 challenge the government to give it to them and allow Canadians to make up their minds who they want to govern them.
The present government does not have a mandate to do what it is doing. I have never heard a Liberal opponent stand on a platform and say, "I will raise the price of gas 80 cents per gallon." I refer to the advertisement of the Minister of Finance which appeared in the January 23, 1980 edition of The Scotia Sun. It was during the election campaign and read:
Because Allan J. MacEachen and the Liberal Party spoke up for you, gas prices came down in December. Vote Liberal and the price will stay down.
That is what the ad said. The Minister of Finance did not even have enough nerve to put in a picture of a Petro-Canada station; he had a picture of a Texaco station. The ad says, "Vote Liberal and the price will stay down". How does he expect the Canadian people to believe him when he campaigned in that manner? After he said that to these people they were alarmed and did not want to be faced with an 18cent increase. They said they would vote for the Minister of Finance because he would keep the price down. That is nonsense.
I will close with this thought, Mr. Speaker. Ottawa today is governing against the traditions of Canada and against the nature of Canada, the interests of Canada and the wishes of Canada. My colleagues are committed to work and build this country and allow the private sector to create permanent jobs

so young people will have a future in Canada. I want to tell you right now Mr. Speaker, that all we need is a chance.
It is time for this government to step aside because of its dismal failure over the last two years. This government has broken all of its election promises with the exception of one. That exception is the $35 a month extra it gave to the old age pensioners. That is the only promise it has kept since the last campaign.
It is time the Prime Minister went to see the Governor General across the road from 24 Sussex to say; "Your Honour, I have been here for 14 years, my crew is tired and they are burnt out. The Minister of Transport"-who I see sitting over there-"is tired and wants a rest. 1 would like you to dissolve Parliament and give the people of Canada an opportunity to elect a government that will set us back on the track of economic and social recovery in this world."

Mr. Speaker, I found the remarks of the hon. member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) rather interesting. Unlike his colleagues, he at least made some suggestions as to how the situation might be improved.
I think the debate during the last couple of weeks has been very negative. Very few positive suggestions have been made. I will try not to be negative when commenting on his suggestions because some were very good. However, one element to his proposals is missing and without it we will have the same basic situation in Canada as exists in the United States. In other words, his recipe sounds very much like Reaganomics.
The hon. member began by accusing the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) of not listening to the business community. He suggested that if he listened to the business community he would find out what he should do. What I find confusing about that suggestion is that the Minister of Finance has listened to the business community. It has told him for the last two years that high interest rates are the prescription for eliminating inflation. That is what the business community and the Chamber of Commerce said to the minister last June. They said, "We must have high interest rates to defeat inflation."
I suggest that the hon. member was not listening to the business community during the last two weeks when the president of the Bank of Montreal, Mr. Mulholland, said that high interest rates are ruining the economy and we must get down to a 12 per cent interest rate. These are the concerns which the business community is talking about and this is what the cabinet and the Minister of Finance are beginning to examine.
Another suggestion was that the budget should be removed as a first step. I admit that the budget does create some problems for the business community, but I have talked to many businessmen during the last six months and they have told me that if it were not for high interest rates the budget would not concern them. They said that the key problem is the cost of money in Canada.
The Minister of Finance is in a very difficult position when he listens to the business community and other groups who say the only way to solve inflation, which they believe to be the
Supply
number one problem, is to reduce the supply of money, which would increase interest rates, slow down the economy and result in a deflationary effect. This may very well be happening to some extent. In fact, the chairman of the Canadian Bankers' Association, for instance, is saying today that inflation rates are probably only 8 per cent rather than lO'/i per cent because we are using the wrong index. In any event, the point I want to make is that the suggestion by the hon. member that the budget is the key issue I do not believe is correct.
In the United States, President Reagan has talked about risk-takers. He has cut taxes in the United States to encourage risk-takers. But the United States is in a real recession and it is bringing the rest of the world down with it. The hon. member discussed relief to those who need it most. The American tax system has been revised many times in the last year in order to give relief to certain areas, but it has still not solved the problem.
The hon. member talked about cutting government spending. There are methods for cutting government spending, but not to any substantial degree. President Reagan has done this but what has happened to the American economy? High interest rates are making it almost impossible for the American economy to move ahead. We are in the same position since the Canadian economy is so dependent on the American economy.
I suggest to the hon. member that if the Tory party does not understand the principle that this is a basic problem which must be faced, then they have no business suggesting that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) should ask the Governor General to call an election. They have no alternative to offer. They have exactly the same to offer as Mr. Reagan proposed for the United States. We see what effect that has had on the world economy.
I would like to discuss in a more analytical way how our country can proceed. It is time we examined our situation seriously. First, I think we must understand some of the problems that are inherent in a high interest rate policy. One detrimental effect of high interest rates is that they are indiscriminate. I think we learn to live with inflation to some extent-although we should not take it for granted-and have come to accept and deal with perhaps a 1 per cent per month increase in inflation. We wither receive more pay or we cut back somewhat on our expenses.
As 1 said, one of the difficulties with inflation is that it does not creep up at 1 per cent or 2 per cent for everyone. For some people inflation increases by 40 per cent or 50 per cent per month while others are not affected for another five years, depending on their financial situation. This situation relates to the business community, the public as well as home owners. It is what I refer to as the indiscriminate effect.
Another aspect of high interest rates is that they tend to be very inflationary. Governor Bouey may deny that by saying that interest rates are only marginally inflationary. While it is difficult to produce figures to prove him wrong, I can produce one set of figures which would give me some reason to believe

May 7, 1982
Supply
that he may very well be wrong. If one takes the base year 1975 and compares it to 1981, it cost Canadians something in the order of $12 billion more than it would have if the currency had remained at the same value as it was in 1975. Our currency having been devalued by approximately 19 per cent, it cost Canadians $12 billion more last year for imports. Also, the difference in interest rates in 1981 as compared to 1975 has cost Canadians $23 billion, which is almost double. In other words, the inflationary effect has been double the effect of the devaluation in the currency. This is a very serious inflationary effect.
Another adverse effect concerns the slowing down of the economy which creates future supply problems. For example, apartment buildings are not being built at a sufficient rate and when interest rates come down we will have some added inflationary effects. Farmers, for instance, who have difficulty maintaining their stock and selling them off at this particular point will cause extreme inflationary effects later on. I have to weigh these problems against the effects of high interest rates.
There is no question but that high inflation is a very serious problem. The argument is not whether we should go after high inflation, but how we should go after it. The government is faced with two possibilities. I think the minister is very seriously looking at these possibilities, as is the government as a whole. The first one deals with the impact which can be made when the Prime Minister goes to the summit along with the Minister of Finance and so on. There can be an impact because it does seem that in this interconnected world, particularly in a country which is as close to the United States as we are, it is very important that our economic policies and American economic policies be roughly on course, since we import perhaps a quarter of everything we use in this country and we export to the same extent and perhaps more than that. So there is a relationship which must be held. Therefore, what happens to the American economy is tremendously important to what is happening to the Canadian economy.
In my own community of Thunder Bay, where we ship 85 per cent or 90 per cent of all of the pulp and paper from our mills to the United States, what the Canadian government does is not really that terribly important. It is what the American economy does that makes Thunder Bay a prosperous community or an unprosperous community. We are not a prosperous community at this particular time simply because the American economy is in a very serious state of affairs.
Let us look at the American economy for a minute because I want to keep referring to our interest rates and American interest rates. The American economy is in a fairly good position in terms of inflation. I do not quite know its present rate, but it looks as though it might have been anywhere around 3 per cent in the last quarter. It may be lower than that. There are some seasonal considerations, but I think we can refer to a 3 per cent or 4 per cent inflation rate.
We have been told by economists from all over that there is a very close relationship between the inflation rate and the interest rate, that the two are parallel. Basically speaking, the
bank prime rate tends to be one, two or three percentage points above the inflation rate over a long period of time. I do not deny this. I have done some work myself and I am sure that is the situation. However, in the United States there is a situation in which the bank prime rate is 16.5 per cent to 17 per cent with an inflation rate of 3 per cent to 4 per cent. So, one is referring to a real interest rate-that is, the prime minus the inflation rate-of 12 per cent. That is four times the norm, the historic norm being 3 per cent.
One can look back to the early fifties and the pattern was there, anywhere from zero per cent to 3 per cent. All of a sudden, the rate is 12 per cent, an increase of four times. In Canada it is probably only about 6 per cent because I would say our inflation rate is 10 per cent or 11 per cent. However, I think an argument can be made that it is only about 8 per cent at this particular point. Therefore, the real rate of interest is six or seven points above, or about double what it should be, historically speaking. If our interest rates are at 8 per cent, then they are nearly triple what they should be.
Therefore, we have this problem and we are beginning to wonder why, if inflation rates start coming down, the interest rates do not come down. The answer must be found in some kind of an analysis of this situation, and there are a number of factors to be considered. One of the major factors in the United States is that the American government will have a deficit of $120 billion, $130 billion or $140 billion. Now, one could say that is no larger, on a ten-to-one ratio, than our deficit, and that is true. It is not any larger on a ten-to-one ratio than our deficit, but it has about double the impact on the United States that it has on Canada simply because the U.S. savings rate is about half the Canadian savings rate. So as a percentage of savings, a $120 billion, a $130 billion or a $140 billion deficit has double the impact it would have on Canada, where we have double the savings. So it is very important to understand that. That deficit will be caused mainly by cutting taxes and introducing the kind of tax incentives to which the hon. members across the aisle are referring, and also by tremendous increases in defence spending. This is one major factor.
Another factor which we as Canadians should be looking at very carefully is the very large demand on the capital market by corporations, many of them large corporations, which are having a great deal of financial difficulty because of the slowness of the economy. They have had to put some real stress on capital markets in order to survive. The amount of borrowing is very large. This is borrowing which would not have occurred if interest rates were lower and the economy were moving faster. These are two very major factors which relate to the capital markets in the United States and in Canada. I do not think that we as Canadians can possibly move in a very substantial way unless we take the factors which are affecting the American economy into consideration.
1 mentioned earlier that we had to deal with two points: one, we must go to the summit and present a very united front against Reaganomics, along with the other six countries. There
May 7, 1982

is a lot of support coming from many elements in the United States, including large segments of the Republican party which feel exactly the same way as we do about this problem. So pressure has been brought to bear on the United States government to get interest rates down and to implement some of the proposals, including cutting the budget, removing some of the defence costs and so on, so that the budget deficit can be brought considerably lower than $100 billion. That is a very important step.
I am sure that our government will take that step but, failing to receive the kind of reaction we want from the American government, then I think we as a government must start winging it alone very soon, this summer or early in the fall. I do not advocate this as a good direction but one which may be necessary if we are to achieve some kind of growth and stimulus in our economy and remove some of the very serious problems that the present economic situation is causing.
I suggest the government take a look at one piece of literature which has come out in the last week, an article in the Financial Times of April 15. The Financial Times commissioned Data Resources, Informetrica Ltd. and the Conference Board of Canada, all three, to see what could happen if the Canadian dollar were allowed to fall to 75 cents. The results from all three were quite remarkable. Roughly speaking, what these three sources have told us is that, in one form or another, we can expect bank prime rates to drop four or five percentage points. We can expect 100,000 new jobs to be created. We can expect some added inflation, perhaps 2 per cent or 3 per cent. This would occur over a fairly short period of time, particularly if this step were taken quickly rather than slowly. These are some of the things that these very informed sources have considered.
I have asked the government to allow, and I know the Minister of Finance is taking a very close look at the possibility of allowing, the dollar to sink to the level of 75 cents U.S., with the idea that we could end up with a 12 per cent interest rate. If hon. members do not believe me, I would ask them to go back and take a good look at this article, because it was a well done study by three reliable economic groups, with good economic models, and they have come up with results which are pretty well parallel. They took different approaches but this is basically what they found.
Does the minister agree with that?
The minister and everyone has seen it and we are very carefully considering it.
Oh!
I think it is time that everyone in the House started to look at it instead of doing things based on the way Reagan is doing things.

Does he agree with you on the Cruise missile?

I would close by saying that a sound policy for this government, which has not been suggested by the opposite side, is to work very hard at the summit to get the American government to do something seriously about the real interest rate which is 12 per cent in the United States, to move in this direction and give some relief for the rest of the world, first of all. And, second, we should take a look at an independent course if that does not work.
If we do not get the response that we and other countries and all kinds of American economists and businessmen and Republicans and Democrats have suggested-if we do not get that response, then we ourselves have to move independently, and I suggest we take a really good look and lower the dollar to about 75 cents, letting it float at this level, increasing the money supply to some extent. I would hope the effect of that would be to lower interest rates as these three studies seem to indicate, to get the rate down to about the 12 per cent level. That would be a tremendous stimulus to the economy and do far more for us than anything which has been suggested from the other side.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the statement he made just now, the hon. Progressive Conservative member has shown once again the inconsistence and incoherence of the Progressive Conservatives. I was saying that they showed they did not know how to count when they failed to make sure there were enough members in the House to have a quorum during the emergency debate. Today, the House is considering an opposition motion requesting the resignation of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, and clearly this is a question that should be important to the Progressive Conservative Party. However, it is strange, Mr. Speaker, that this Opposition motion is so important that the Progressive Conservatives are not even asking for a vote.
They want the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to resign, but they do not want to get into a situation where they would have to vote on the question. They are prepared to have a debate today on this bit of wishful thinking, but they are not prepared to ask the House to vote on the question. Earlier this week I said that the cow that moos the most gives the least milk. Well, 1 just heard one mooing on the opposite side, and it probably is one of the best specimens of this kind of animal we know so well.
If we look at our economic and energy policies, it is easy to understand why the Progressive Conservative party is not asking for a vote on this motion today. The reason is quite simple: they have no alternative solutions, either for energy or for economic problem. Should my hon. colleagues opposite be reluctant to take my word for it, and before my hon. colleague for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) loses his temper, claiming I have no proof, I would refer him to an article published this week on May 4 in La Presse, in which the Leader of the Opposition had given an interview. The article was signed by Alain Dubuc and a partial quote from page 3 reads as follows:
In an interview he gave yesterday to a group of reporters from La Presse, the Leader of the Opposition, Joe Clark, made the most astounding and disarming statement ever made by an opposition leader, when he acknowledged that his party had found no alternative to the Bank of Canada's economic policy.
And here we have a quote from what was said by the Leader of the Opposition.
We have looked for alternatives to the government's policies, but we have found none, he acknowledged.
Another quote.
Today, I have no better solution.
That is the Progressive Conservative record on economic policy and on energy policy. We know, Mr. Speaker, and it is even worse, because we know what they did and what they tried to do when they were in power for a few months. This week, we listened for hours to their complaints, their criticisms, their insults and their interruptions during the debate; but solutions? Not a sign. The other side is capable only of creating obstruction and criticizing, but it can never come up with positive and constructive proposals. Conversely, I should like to point out that in the energy sector, this government has implemented some very important measures during the past two years it has been in power.
With respect to energy security, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to mention that despite the abandonment of the Alsands project, Canada today is in a far more comfortable situation as far as energy security is concerned than it was when the present government came to power in 1980. I wish to emphasize that on the Alsands project we had the best possible cooperation from the government of Alberta, and both governments made a joint offer to the private sector companies involved which even the companies had to admit was very generous. However, for reasons of their own, the companies decided they could not take a chance on such a large-scale project at this time. Incidentally, during the same week, in the United States where there is no program similar to the Canadian one, during that same week, Exxon, the biggest multinational in the world, abandoned a project in which the company had already invested $1 billion, and also at the same time, the promoters of the Alaska pipeline project decided to postpone the project for two years. Throughout our negotiations, the government of Alberta and the Government of Canada have said that there was a limit to the demands that
May 7, 1982

could be made on Canadian consumers and taxpayers for the purpose of operating or building a project. If we exceeded those limits, we would be acting irresponsibly in spending the Canadian taxpayers' money. In fact, both the government of Alberta and the Government of Canada have acted responsibly in this regard, and once again, the long-drawn-out complaints of the official opposition are no substitute for the responsible policies required in these circumstances.
I said we would succeed, and that our energy security, particularly as far as oil is concerned, is in better shape today than it was when the Progressive Conservatives were defeated, thank God and thank the voters in February 1980. When the Leader of the Official Opposition attended the summit meeting in Tokyo as Prime Minister, he promised to maintain crude oil imports at 600,000 barrels per day or less. Actually, we are going to do a lot better. In 1981, we imported only 509,000 barrels of oil per day, which is well under the maximum set by the Leader of the Official Opposition at the time. In 1985, we shall be importing less than 300,000 barrels per day. How are we going to do this? Well, by increasing production of Canadian oil. It is interesting to note that this year, for the first time in almost a decade, the Canadian Petroleum Association was able to announce an increase in Canada's oil reserves over the previous years. Before, every year, Canada's oil reserves had been diminishing. This year, for the first time, our reserves have increased, according to the figures of the Canadian Petroleum Association.
Other ways of achieving energy security, in addition to increasing reserves and production, are to reduce oil consumption through conservation and replacement of oil by other forms of energy. In fact, our off-oil program implemented not quite a year ago to encourage Canadians to substitute other forms of energy for oil, especially for home-heating, has already produced remarkable results. This is in addition to our insulation program. Our off-oil program provides grants of $800 per household to change heating systems. Our home insulation program is paying up to $500 per household. And what are the results of all this? Well, in 1981, consumption of crude oil in Canada dropped by 7 per cent. Consumption of heating oil has dropped by 17 per cent and that of heavy fuel oil by 13 per cent over the same period.
These results are facts, and between 1980 and the end of 1982, oil consumption in Canada is expected to drop by almost 15 per cent. These figures are authentic and well-known, and they demonstrate the success of our policy to reduce oil consumption while at the same time increasing reserves for the future. In fact, a few weeks ago we announced an extension of the home insulation program, so that now, all homes built before 1971 will be eligible for the insulation program and thus for the $500 grant provided by law. This will add more than one million homes to the list of those eligible for these grants, and, directly or indirectly, we will create about 20,000
Supply
jobs this year, if consumers are willing to make use of the program and benefit from energy savings. That is, consumers who are willing to make use of the program, as more than a million have already done during the last two years, will save on their energy bills or at least these bills will increase very little, even if the price of energy continues to rise substantially over the next four or five years. Conservation is still the best way to ensure self-sufficiency for Canada in coming years.
And if the members opposite doubt the effectiveness of our policy in this regard, I would ask them to refer to a report of the International Energy Agency, which includes all the industrialized countries except France. This agency stated the following:
Until now, only a few countries have developed specific policies to promote oil replacement. With its oil replacement program launched in October 1980, Canada is the only OECD country to have set up a full and comprehensive conversion policy aimed at all the sectors which use oil products, by setting oil consumption reduction objectives and providing financial assistance.
This statement was made by the International Energy Agency. As I have already stated, we also have some good news concerning supplies. The reserves forecast by the Canadian Petroleum Association in 1981 have increased, practically for the first time in ten years. The news is extremely encouraging with regard to the potential production offshore, in the Beaufort Sea and in the Arctic. Of course, our critics opposite will not want to recognize this reality. As I mentioned earlier, they are simply obsessed by the idea that the government should give even more money to the companies and that the National Energy Program is supposedly stifling these companies. Mr. Speaker, I would like to look at what has happened to a number of companies, for instance the major multinationals and their Canadian subsidiaries, in 1980 and 1981. In seven out of eight cases, the Canadian subsidiaries had higher earnings in 1980 and 1981 than the foreign-owned multinational parent company.
In 1980, for instance, the first four on the list were as follows: Texaco-I am speaking about the parent company- had an increase of 27 per cent while its Canadian subsidiary had an increase of 41 per cent. Gulf had an increase of 6 per cent while its Canadian subsidiary had an increase of 33 per cent. Royal Dutch Shell showed an international decrease of 27 per cent while its Canadian subsidiary showed an increase of 37 per cent. Exxon had an increase of 31 per cent while the Canadian subsidiary, Imperial Oil, had an increase of 38 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I wonder if the minister would identify the source of his figures respecting increases in Canadian profits. 1 think he will find that the profits do not come from the producing end. Those profits are down distinctly. That is what we are concerned about. Profits on the retail side are up significantly, and that is because of the huge amounts of taxes the government is taking.

Mr. Speaker, I hope you will reduce from my time all the irrelevant points of order we have heard during my speech. If the House so wishes, I would be very happy to answer questions later. I will have no problem answering any question the hon. member wants to raise.
With respect to the point raised by the hon. member, 1 point out to him that whether the money comes from upstream or downstream, if a company has more profits it has more money to do whatever it wants to do. That is the point we are discussing.
[ Translation]
I will continue, Mr. Speaker. The Conservatives do not like to hear those figures because they are so used to go to bed with multinational and big oil companies that they are totally blind to reality and that every time an attempt is made to put the facts straight, they take it personal.
This is what happened in 1981. Texaco International increased its revenues by 7 per cent; its Canadian subsidiary by nearly 9 per cent; exactly 8.9 per cent. Gulf showed a profit loss of 17 per cent; its Canadian subsidiary indicated a profit loss of 11.8 per cent. Royal Dutch had a loss in its international operations of under 70 per cent, its Canadian subsidiary registered a loss of less than 15 per cent. The only international company, in 1981, according to the list I have mentioned, where the parent company did better than its Canadian subsidiary, is EXXON which showed an increase of more than 11 percent, and Imperial with a loss of less than 10 per cent. However, I would remind you that the year before the situation was reversed and the Canadian subsidiary had done better than the parent company. Of course, the Conservative opposition is not interested in hearing those figures but perhaps they might like to recognize at least that a large number of Canadian companies have tremendous investment projects in Canada this year. I should simply like to mention Canterra, a Canadian company which expects to spend $500 million in 1982 in exploration alone, and Gulf which over the next five years expects to invest $7 billion in Canada and Petro-Canada which has set aside a budget of $450 million for exploration and development alone in western Canada. These data are known to everyone except, it seems, to the opposition.
And, to assist them, I can already indicate that next week we will be in a position to announce new developments involving multinational companies and Canadian companies which, over the next years, will announce huge investments in the field of research and additional oil resources in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I only have a few minutes left, I will conclude simply by suggesting that over that period we succeeded in increasing Canadian oil ownership to a significant degree. Foreign ownership over the last 18 months declined from 72 per cent to 65.4 per cent, or more than 6 per cent, with an increase in Canadian ownership of more than 6 per cent. Foreign control in that area declined from 77 per cent to 67 per cent, a 10 per cent decrease in favour of Canadians. Such measures were successful and will continue to be so over the coming years.
The last aspect is the matter of price. We implemented a pricing system that is fair to the consumer and that any way will be lower over that period than that provided for by the Progressive Conservatives in their famous budget. Some say that currently we pay more for gas in Canada than in the United States. It is important to remember, in the first place that as far as home-heating oil is concerned, it sells much cheaper here than in the United States, up to 7 cents less per litre. As far as natural gas is concerned, our costs are tremendously lower than in the United States. As for gas, this varies from province to province. In Alberta, the price of a litre of gas is less than in Chicago, but in Montreal it is more expensive than in New York. The reason is quite simple, there is no provincial tax in Alberta, while Quebec levies up to 13 cents per litre, the highest in Canada. So there is no mystery there. The barrel of oil coming to a refinery in Canada currently costs only 71 per cent of the oil price, or to practical purposes 71 per cent of the American price. When the price of a gallon or litre of gas sold at the pump is higher than in United States, the answer is in the provincial tax that each provincial government decides to levy. Again, for proof one has only to take the province levying no provincial tax, where the litre of gas is cheaper than in United States. These are facts that my Conservative colleagues will not recognize, because as I said, rather than listen, analyse, read and study, they would rather moo in this House and elsewhere, like the cow I was referring to.

Mr. Speaker, it is incredible to hear the minister defend an energy policy which is a disaster and is destroying the economic fibre of our country. He boasts about it.
At this critical juncture in the political and economic life of the country I am proud that it is this party's action that has afforded Canadians the opportunity today to learn more fully about the criminal ineptitude of the government.
Not only have Canadians been sent reeling by record interest rates, rampant inflation, and the highest unemployment since the 1930s-the latest figures that I have seen for the Niagara Peninsula show 15.6 per cent unemployment-but now they have to suffer the death of the one bright hope that we had in the country, the Alsands project. Energy megaprojects have been touted to guarantee energy self-sufficiency, to provide employment for up to 100,000 Canadians, and to stimulate the economies not only of the producing provinces but of the manufacturing and industrial sectors of central Canada.
The Liberal government pointed with pride to the megaprojects as an engine that would pull Canada from its economic doldrums. The government's political skin is at risk as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) tries to twist and turn the truth, and as the Minister of Finance
May 7, 1982

(Mr. MacEachen) clouds the issue with his customary obfuscation in an attempt to muddy the waters and throw the blame for the collapse of the Alsands project elsewhere.
The Liberals have built their economic policies on sand, and that sand has turned into quicksand. Now those policies have been exposed for the sham and illusion they are. What a shame that is-it is a shameful sham! The Grits really needed some cheery news to save their cookies but this was not to be. It is all their own fault. Their inflexible attitude, their intransigence, their misbegotten and woebegone, ill conceived National Energy Program, that the minister spoke of in the House today, is to blame for the mess. In fact one journalist called it a "megamess". That is the mess in which they now find themselves. Liberal members of the House know that. Unfortunately, Canada suffers as a result of Liberal misjudgment, Liberal mismanagement, and Liberal mistakes.
Liberal mismanagement of the economy has resulted in corporate profits being 44 per cent lower in the fourth quarter of 1981 than in the fourth quarter of 1982. I suppose I should be careful when mentioning profit because members of the NDP do not like the word. But I will mention the word profit; it is what is needed in the economy as an incentive to get things going again.
Manufacturing is at 75 per cent capacity, the lowest level capacity utilization in 20 years. The primary metals industry is operating at 65 per cent of capacity. The transportation equipment industry is operating at 54 per cent capacity. The wood industry upon which the province of British Columbia is so dependent is operating at 57 per cent. This underutilization has led to a net loss of 127,000 jobs in the manufacturing sector of the economy, since August. Many of those jobs have been lost in my own province of Ontario, many of them in my own riding and the Niagara Peninsula. In March of this year a record 1.2 million Canadians were without work. In the same month the inflation rate was 11.6 per cent.
The outrage with which the budget was greeted, Mr. Speaker, led the Minister of Finance to retreat in some areas, and temper his policies in others, but the over-all thrust of the government remains the same: massive restructuring of tax laws without consultation with the private sector and, apparently, without thought for the consequences. The outrage continues. This budget is distinguished only by the fact that it has drawn together so many diverse groups. They are now united in opposition to the government's draconian measures. Yet, in spite of the anger and resentment directed against the government, the minister is stubborn in his determination to make no further changes. Even Walter Gordon, renowned for his facility in the preparation of budgets, has said:
No government, no Minister of Finance, should be reluctant to consider and revise proposals if public discussion shows it to be desirable.
Interest rates are in the stratosphere. The U.S. sends men to the moon; we send interest rates into the stratosphere, this from a government which promised to "manage the economy in such a way that interest rates would in fact come down .. .
Supply
because the economy would be administered in a sounder way". They have yet to prove that.
These worries are compounded, Mr. Speaker, by the collapse of the $13.5 billion Alsands project which could have delivered 137,000 barrels a day of Canadian oil, bringing us much closer to self-sufficiency and oil security. It would have reduced unemployment, increased manufacturing, and meant an input of $450 billion into our economy. Yet Alsands died and the question is: why? Why? That is the question which Canadians need to be asking and are asking today. That is the question hon. members opposite need to be asking. The answer is simple. The National Energy Program is the culprit and its perpetrators, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, have yet another disaster on their consciences. I am of course, giving them the benefit of the doubt by assuming they have consciences.
The NEP was a revenue grab. It thrust the government into private enterprise where it has no business being. It discriminates against foreign petroleum rights, it breaks all the ground rules and sets new ones without the benefit of consultation. The result of this massive interference in the marketplace was industry mistrust of the federal government typified in a statement by John Stoik, president of Gulf Canada, who said:
Over the years the government has so strained its credibility with retroactive rule changes that those of us in the industry must ask ourselves, how can we undertake to make huge investments in long-term megaprojects when we have good reason to fear that the government will come along again and pull the rug on us?
The NEP has so restricted cash flow that oil and gas companies are simply unable to make large-scale equity investments. Under the present circumstances of inflation and high interest rates it is utterly impossible for oil and gas companies to go to the market for debt capital.
The NEP is destroying our energy potential. It will mean the loss of billions of dollars which are simply drifting across the border into the U.S., the northern part of South America, and the Middle East. It will literally cost us hundreds of thousands of jobs. The two tar sands plants will not continue development because the minister was not able to negotiate a pricing arrangement on oil. This means a loss to Ontario of $108 billion over the 25-year life of just one tar sands plant. One plant! Hon. members will bear in mind that we require nine plants if we are to reach energy self-sufficiency.
To start development on one plant would mean an infusion of $800 million into the economy of Ontario through the iron and steel industry, but this government said no. Such a development would create $370 million in the metal fabrication and machinery industries of Ontario. Many of my constituents work in the city of Welland. Pipe is manufactured there, and these projects would have been a great stimulus to that industry. Once again the government has denied my province, that city, and other areas this opportunity. This development would create an additional $325 million in sales for the transportation equipment industry. This development would mean $750 million for Ontario in trades and services.

May 7, 1982
