The most effective way for Alsands to have remained a viable component of the Canadian economy would have been to allow, indeed restore, a system in which private industry could earn adequate profits and generate its own risk capital. Without the NEP and a more flexible and helpful attitude on the part of the federal government, Alsands would now be well under way. In fact, under a Tory government it would have been well under way.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the tragedy is that no matter how great a death blow the collapse of the Alsands project is, the NEP has claimed other victims, thereby compounding its effect. Cold Lake is dead; the Esso Resources Judy Creek recovery project has been cancelled; Syncrude expansion plans have been terminated. There were three occasions when the Liberal government fumbled and lost the good will of the consortium. In March, 1980, the government declared the world price for oil would no longer be paid for oil sands production. The industry interpretation of this announcement was that the government was not interested in oil sands.
In October, 1980, the inception of the NEP again caused industry to believe the government was not serious. The energy pricing agreement of September, 1981, did little to allay those fears. What are the results of the demise of the Alsands project, aside from those already mentioned? For one thing the Canadian dollar fell by half a cent. The loss in investment will mean that the gross national expenditure will be lower by 1.8 per cent. Employment in 1990 will be lower by 153,000 Canadians. At the same time the current account deficit will have deteriorated by $9.7 billion. Furthermore, Canadian selfsufficiency in energy is doomed. The death of the megaprojects means there will be a total loss of 350,000 barrels of oil a day, oil which could have been produced in Canada.
It appears, Mr. Speaker, that not only the maritimes will have to continue to rely on imported oil; by 1990, Toronto will be in the same position. The upshot of this is that the federal government is subsidizing the importation of a very large volume of foreign crude oil while an equivalent volume is available but is not being produced in western Canada. Instead that oil has been shut-in. The government has been importing foreign crude on an increasing scale for some time, and the volume involved is inevitably going to grow rather than decline.
There is a heavy cost in public funds through the subsidies being paid on the foreign oil. This heavy cost would disappear if the foreign oil were replaced by domestic supplies that are available. There is an economic cost in addition. Large amounts of money are leaving the country, where they can have no further effect on the Canadian economy, while that same money, if it were spent on western oil, would naturally recirculate and produce economic activity, activity that we so desperately need.
The lesson to be learned from state intervention in the oil industry is simple we think. Not even someone as self confident as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is able to foresee all of the complexities of an industry and the shifting market forces that affect it. The elaborate control mechanisms of the National Energy Program are, of necessity, rigid. The process of adaptation to unforeseen circumstances is slow and creaking. The larger question behind all of this revolves around the real purpose of the Prime Minister's championing of the National Energy Program. We all remember his interview in which he discussed his efforts to change the course of the ship of state. This is a part of it:
One has to be in the wheelhouse to see what shifts are taking place. I know that we have spun the wheel and I know that the rudder is beginning to press against the waves and the sea. But perhaps the observer, who is on the deck and smoking his pipe, or drinking his tea, sees the horizon much in the same direction and doesn't realize it, but perhaps he will find himself disembarking at a different island than the one he thought he was sailing for.
What do these musings mean when seen in the context of the National Energy Program and the havoc it has wrought on the oil and gas industry and on megaprojects, such as Alsands and Cold Lake? Speculation is one thing, but the facts speak for themselves. After the NEP was introduced in October, 1980, and up to January, 1982, a total of 272 drilling rigs left Canada. The replacement value of these rigs is $1.1 billion. The other damage caused by the NEP 1 have already discussed-yes, and the NDP as well. Surely these negative results were readily foreseeable.
Why then was the NEP forced on an unwilling industry and on reluctant provinces? Does the Prime Minister have some darker, ulterior motive than the one so simple, so-called Canadianization. And if so, what is that purpose? Could it be that he desires total state intervention in the oil and gas business? If that be the case, where do his ambitions end, and down what rocky road is he leading Canada?
Speaking about entrepreneurship, Professor Raymond Kao of Ryerson Polytechnical Institute, said:
Entrepreneurs are not ones who like to face reality. They create reality. Since they create reality, they want to create it at an early age-high school age. We should be encouraging them even then.
Entrepreneurship is being destroyed by a government that is foisting socialism and the other policies it has upon our nation. This government is taking away the entrepreneurial attitude and spirit that have built this country, that have caused our young people to go out and invest, that have caused our older people to go out and invest and build businesses. In a country like Canada where the population is small and the land is vast, government has an important role to play. No one denies that, but massive unthinking government intervention has eroded Canadians' confidence and it will be a long, slow, tortuous job to rekindle that confidence. Quite frankly, I cannot see the present government even making an attempt. What we have to get back and what we need to get back is that essential trust and good will which the present government has frittered away.

Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to hear the speech of the hon. member for Erie (Mr. May 7, 1982

Fretz). Last year at about exactly this time he was with me on the "Metres for Millions" march. We made it half way. The "Metres for Millions" march is on tomorrow, and I would encourage all hon. members to be out walking through my riding of Ottawa Centre, through Nepean-Carleton, and through Ottawa-Vanier.
I was very interested in the speech which my friend from Erie made. It was a pretty reasonable speech. The hon. member did put forward some suggestions. The basic thrust was at the end of his speech. He stressed the importance of the confidence factor in this country, the importance of investor confidence and the importance of worker confidence. I do not want to get into the partisan issues that are normally thrown around in this House, but yesterday was an example of a situation where hon. members threw mud back and forth at each other in this House, so I hope there can be some positive suggestions and dialogue in this debate today.
I hope in our debates in the future that we can build on a spirit of trying to do something constructive in this House as opposed to what, unfortunately, has characterized many of the debates in the last few months. It does not do any of us any good. It certainly does no good for the people of the country.
In this debate we should be trying to examine as carefully as possible the exact nature of the economic situation which faces us. We should be trying to look for positive solutions to help Canada position herself more effectively to participate in the recovery that is going to come in the world economy. Then we would be in a better position to move ahead with growth, job creation and wealth creation, when that happens here. I for one am confident that if we are not at the bottom of the recession we are very near to it. I believe that we are about to see the break in the inflation rate that we have all been waiting for, and that we are about to see the beginnings of job creation rather than job destruction. I think we have come very close to the bottom of this terrible situation that we have been facing these past many months.
All of us in this House of Commons have decried the situation. We have all wished that we did not have to go through it. We have all wished that the world market for our minerals, timber, oil, automobiles and other products had not fallen apart the way it did. All of us agree that if the Alsands project could have gone ahead it would have been a great thing for Canada. But I want to say one thing about Alsands. I think there is a myopia taking place in this House that does not necessarily have to be the case.
The investment dollars that were going to be put into the Alsands plant have not evaporated. They have not disappeared. Shell, Gulf, and the other private sector companies in the consortium did not take that money and burn it.
It has been taxed away.

That money has not gone. There was to be $14 billion of investment. What happened? The private sector companies looked at the economics and concluded that the economics did not make sense. Therefore, they decided not to invest that money. The money is still there, the borrowing
Supply
potential is still there, and the investment funds are still there. These companies and the government will be able to employ those funds in other areas of the economy. If Alsands is not built, certainly other projects will be built which would not have otherwise had access to capital. The money did not evaporate; it is not as though it were burned. The potential is still there and the projects are still there. Canada still has the potential it had yesterday. It has not gone away. That investment will take place, perhaps in other sectors, but it will take place.
I should like to look at the situation as I see it, and to put forward my assessment of what we should do to position ourselves properly to take advantage of the growth and development of job creation, wealth creation, and rising standards of living which we have every right to expect in Canada. We must come to grips with issues revolving around three major sets of alternatives.
First, we should look at the question of what is the proper balance for government between distribution and creation. Those are the alternatives. We can focus all our attention on the redistribution of wealth, or we can refocus our attention more toward the creation of wealth, which gives us more to redistribute at a later date. The second factor is the balance between savings and consumption. We should rebalance some of our priority away from current consumption expenditures and toward savings and investment. After all, this will be the engine by which we generate economic growth and rising standards of living in the future. The third and most important factor I want to discuss today is the attitude or the confidence factor, which is the balance between the preservation of the status quo and the orientation toward the future.
It is natural during times of economic decline, recession, high inflation and high unemployment, for people, countries, parliaments, and especially politicians, to begin to look inward, to focus their attention upon how they can protect what they now have and to forget about the kinds of activities which they must undertake if they are to realize the potential of the future. The time is now for us to begin to turn our attention away from the preservation and protection of the status quo toward the generation and creation of the great future which Canada can have. But it will require a shifting of priorities in the country and that we all sacrifice a bit on consumption to put a bit more toward savings which will generate investment. Also it will require that we think more in terms of the creation of wealth as opposed to the distribution of wealth. These are terribly important concepts. Canada is at the spot where decisions such as these must be made.
You cannot distribute what you do not create.

1 hear the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro). That is precisely the message I am trying to put across to the opposition today. We must refocus our attention-

Supply
But you are not.

The hon. member complains that we are not doing it. I try to remove myself, whenever I can, from the partisan haranguing in the House. I try not to fight about what they are saying, and 1 prefer if they do not fight about what I am saying. That is not the point of Parliament. We are in Parliament together. We are expected by the people of the country to work together in Parliament, and we had better start working together.
You had better start listening.

The hon. member is suggesting that I should listen to him. Perhaps he will listen to me. I will listen to him if he listens to me. As a government we sit here day after day, listening to members of the opposition saying that we must create wealth before we can distribute it. But in the same breath they say, "Oh, by the way, we want quotas on footwear and on automotive products." They indicate that they want this for this industry and that for that industry; that they want protection for this and that group. I think the hon. member and I agree that governments basically distribute. Apart from Crown corporations which have creative functions, such as Petro-Canada and Canadair, governments are basically redistributive mechanisms. They do not create anything, they distribute.
Good. We have you on the record on that.

We agree on that. The opposition benches continually harangue day after day by telling the government, on the one hand, that we need less government expenditures and more room for the private sector-and I agree with that- and on the other hand by saying that we must protect various groups and give more money here and there. We cannot do that. We cannot do both things at the same time. If we agree-and I think we do-that governments are basically a redistributive mechanism, then if governments do not create wealth and the money that is distributed, it must come from somewhere. From where does it come? It comes from taxpayers, or from people in some other way. We obtain the money we spend by generating higher levels of inflation, by generating higher interest rates because we must borrow the money in capital markets, or by taxing it. This is done in the government sector.
Other activities which are undertaken by government are equally as redistributive. Hon. members opposite keep demanding these kinds of policies. They are saying that we should have protection, quotas and tariffs. Hon. members opposite are the party of protectionism. It is not this party, but that party. Protectionism is just as much a form of tax on Canadians as a direct tax levy by government. If I put a tariff on an item and force consumers to pay a higher price than otherwise, is it not a redistribution? Certainly it is. Therefore I
May 7, 1982
say all the actions of governments-whether they are Conservative ones in Manitoba, now NDP, NDP ones in Saskatchewan, now Conservative, or whatever-involve redistribution.
All of us in the House have not paid enough attention to the following questions: from whom are we distributing, and to whom are we distributing? Wealth is not destroyed or created; it is just redistributed. We must look at these questions extremely carefully. If we are to have investment, growth, higher productivity and lower inflation in the country, we must undertake some very positive redistributive policies of a certain nature and in a certain direction. It would be very useful and helpful to government if the opposition would indicate consistently which direction it would like to see that redistribution take. As I said, oftentimes the opposition is inconsistent. First it says that the wealth should be distributed this way; then it says it should be redistributed another way. This is not helpful at all.
Opposition members ask why I do not listen to what they are saying. It is because they say one thing on one day and another thing another day. One does not make long-term economic policy on the basis of daily shifts of view.
Thank you, Kenneth Galbraith.

1 am afraid my hon. friend has the wrong economist. Hon. members opposite are having some fun with me; I am glad to see the Acting Speaker, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, is now in a position where he cannot.
I have to bring to the attention of the hon. members opposite a very lucid point which was raised by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition. (Mr. Clark). In a recent interview with La Presse in Montreal, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition said, with candour and honesty, "I do not know what the answer is either. We do not have an alternative solution to what the government is doing." That is precisely what he said and it is in the press and on the record. He was being honest. He said, "We do not have an alternative economic policy to the government's policy."
That is not what he said.
The article is in my briefcase in case the hon. member wants me to pull it out. It went on the record the other day when I quoted it on a Standing Order 43.
Pull it out.
Tell us about the budget.
The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) is back.
Tell us about the budget.

The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Wright) is here also. Tweedledee and Tweedledum are both here and that is good.
May 7, 1982

Let me give some thoughts on specific policies which I think must be examined very carefully and on which we must move forward. We must implement these policies if we are to put ourselves in a position for the economic recovery which is coming. There is no doubt that we have to bring down the rate of inflation and 1 do not think there is any disagreement that without a reduction in inflation we will have great difficulty in participating in investment for the future. High inflation tends to shorten your time and you do not make long-term investment decisions in that environment.
I believe we must also be concerned about restraining the growth in the cost of production in our society. As well, we must be concerned about the rise in wages and prices in our economy. Apart from the inflationary price increases, the rise in the cost structure in our society is terribly perplexing at the moment. It could put us in non-competitive situation with the rest of the world.
I think it is clear-and the budget attempted to move in this direction-that we have to reduce the budget deficit of the government and bring down the exposure of the government in the capital markets in order to leave more room for the private sector at more reasonable rates of interest than we face now. I also think that we have to find policies which will stimulate savings and thereby stimulate investment in our economy and increase productivity as well. We have to alter the reward structure and put policies in place which will create those favourable conditions.
I think the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) was absolutely correct when he said in his speech that we have to restore investor and worker confidence. That is essential. Those are five suggestions.
We must examine our policies and the mix of federal and provincial policies to consider whether we have policies in place which act as a disincentive to productive activity by individuals or corporations.
Finally, I put forward the call that we should be looking, at this point in time, at the whole question of the impact of our tax system on economic activity and individual behaviour. I think it is time for another commission to review the performance of the tax system. Our tax system is serving many purposes at the present time. At one time it was a revenue-raising device. It then became a wealth redistribution device and subsequently it became an economic activity-generating device. Right now, the tax system is being used to perform so many functions that it is not clear what or how well it is doing. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the kind of simplification measures which were put forward in the budget were a step in the direction of clarifying the tax system and lowering tax rates.
What are you going to do about this budget?

The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona is at it again, Mr. Speaker. The howling monkey from Edmonton-Strathcona.
I believe that these are important steps which all members should be working at achieving as a Parliament. I think they
Business of the House
are in the best interests of the Canadian people. These steps will put the system in a position to develop and grow at its optimal and not lag behind the rest of the world.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to seize this opportunity to designate next Friday as an allotted day. Therefore, next week there will be two allotted days, Tuesday and Friday.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. McGrath:
That this House, caring for the 1,200,000 Canadians now unemployed and the millions more worried about their jobs, recognizes that the National Energy Program and the budgets of October, 1980, and November, 1981, are largely responsible for this massive unemployment, and demands the resignations of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Finance and the introduction of a new energy policy and a new budget to create jobs, lower interest rates and restore hope and confidence to Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, before I get into the discussion, I would like to say I was rather interested in what the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) had to say, because if I correctly understand him, he has split Bill C-93, which is what we have been requesting for some time. This bill is very similar to the energy bill which caused the problem and the ringing of the bells some weeks back.
It is marvellous how lessons are learned.

I am very pleased at what the President of the Privy Council has done. He showed good sense for a change and we hope that will continue into the future.
The topic today is the motion presented by my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). The topic basically deals with unemployment, the budget, interest rates, energy and the confidence of this government. I shall go into all those topics as 1 go along.
The economy of Canada is in a tough way. These are hard times for the people of Canada.
Liberal times are hard times.

They are rapidly being known as Grit times. Hard times will be known for years afterward as Grit times.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) stood in this House and said he had a strategy. He is a leading spokesman for the government today. Where is his strategy? It is not in the budget and it is not in the energy policy. It is certainly not in the housing policy and it is certainly not in the employment policy.
It was not in his speech, either.

This government has no policy except to make it difficult for all Canadians. This is a time of high inflation, high interest rates and high unemployment. The people of Canada will remember for many years the way in which the government did them in.
Strategy tragedy.

This government, instead of having an over-all strategy, intends only to band-aid this economy back to health, providing little help, not much; but every once in a while it will help in a very small way. If we think back to 1974, the government said it had inflation under control. In 1976 it changed monetary policies, and inflation has become worse ever since. In 1974 it said we would reach energy self-sufficiency by 1980, but we obviously have not reached energy self-sufficiency and many people say we will not have it by 1990.
In 1974 the government told us there would be no wage and price controls. The Liberals were elected under that promise and we had wage and price controls one year hence. This government does not live up to its promises.
If we look at the expenditures of the government at the present time, we find that the government spends 25 per cent more than it takes in. That is why we have inflation in Canada; there is no other reason. We find the government spends 20 cents out of every dollar on servicing the national debt. That is why we have inflation, not for any other reason. It is not because of interest rates in the United States or because of anything else the Canadian people are doing. It is because of government policies.
These are hard times. We should consider the unemployment figures in Canada. The Minister of Employment and Immigration stood in the House and said things are not that bad in many areas, but as we look across Canada we can see the unemployment. Ontario has an unemployment rate of 10.5 per cent in the manufacturing industry, compared to 6.4 per cent a year ago. It is getting worse all the time. If we look at the fishing industry on the east and west coast, we find that in Atlantic Canada the unemployment rate is 14 per cent compared to 11.8 per cent last year, and in B.C. the unemployment rate is 17.8 per cent compared to 10.5 per cent last year. This is all due to this government's policies, there is no other reason. If we look at the forestry industry, we find 46.7 per cent unemployment in Atlantic Canada. Standing in this House within the last week, I said that the unemployment rate in forestry in Atlantic Canada was approximately 50 per cent
May 7, 1982

and the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) said that was not so. I am now presenting statistics.
In B.C. the unemployment rate in the forestry industry is 30.6 per cent compared to 29 per cent one year ago. In Quebec the unemployment rate in mining today is 28.7 per cent compared 12.6 per cent. That is another point which, of course, the hon. member for Ottawa Centre denied.
The unemployment rate across Canada in various segments of the economy is a disaster. We look at the unemployment figures across Canada for all industries and find that it is 9 per cent and rising. There are 1.2 million unemployed people. It is said that there are an additional 300,000 or 400,000 people who are not even registered; they cannot find jobs and have given up. That is the type of government we have. That is the type of planning we get from this government. That is the government's strategy.
Where is the housing policy in Canada? What kind of housing policy do we have? We have a Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) who stands in this House and says, "We have a solution: Bill C-89 will be the solution for the housing problems of Canada." That measure was introduced in the budget on November 12, but we still have not seen any solution to the housing problems.
Let us look at some of those problems. At the present time, the adjusted annual rate of starts is 142,000 units in Canada. If we break that down, we find that urban housing starts in April of this year, compared to last year, were down 40 per cent. Single detached dwelling starts were down 61 per cent and multi-unit starts were down 19 per cent. Where is the housing policy which was promised us? It is not doing any good. Statistics Canada indicates we need starts of 200,000 units each year. What does CMHC say we will have? There will be 146,000 units built this year. That is the estimate. So 54,000 more units should be built, representing almost 100,000 jobs.
The Minister of Public Works stands in this House and says he will help create employment. He will increase employment in the housing industry. He is not doing anything. Why is he not doing anything? If we look at the estimates we find, for example, that foreign aid has gone up by 19 per cent this year to over $1 billion, at a time when people are losing their homes, when people cannot renew their mortgages, when rents are going up. Why are we increasing foreign aid at this time? Why are we spending S70 million a year on advertising so Canadians will know what the government wants to do? Why is that money not put into housing, which will have a direct effect on employment? No, the government does not want to do those things because, in reality, it does not have a strategy or a plan. If does not really want to help. By having this grand design of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)-whatever it is- he will help someone, but he does not provide the help where it is needed at the right time. Those statistics show that the budget strategy of this government is non-existent.
If we look at the recent Conference Board report we find that the statistics get even worse. We should look specifically
Supply
at Ontario, the province which is suffering more this year. The Conference Board of Canada states that Ontario has been given one of its worst economic report cards in a decade. This is the board which warned last week that Canadians can expect no relief from the recession until at least next year. It has added an even more sombre footnote in that it says in its report that in the last year the economy has changed so much that it will represent the most severe setback in decades. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) stands in this House and says that is not true. Mr. Speaker, the Conference Board goes on to say that the decline in the economy is not only steep but widespread. That is another point that the Minister of Finance denies in this House.
The conference board goes on to say that while the 1980 decline in Ontario production was due to the automotive industry, in 1981, it was more widespread and affected all segments of the Ontario economy. This is the type of thing the government presents to us and tells us how well they are doing. These certainly are hard times and they will get worse as long as we have this government in power.
If we look back at that budget presented on November 12, 1981, we find the Minister of Finance saying that tax incentives offered to Canadians are now tax loopholes. Obviously they left some tax incentives but the average Canadian has to ask himself or herself: "When is the government going to strike against me; when is it going to take away my tax incentives?"
The question of imputed rent has been brought to the attention of the government. The government attempted to back off from that. Why do they attempt to back off? The reason is that 50 per cent of the people in Canada own their own homes. What would happen if only 25 per cent of the people owned their own homes? Then they would not have to worry about imputed rent; that would be the time to bring it in. We are bringing to the attention of the Canadian public what the government was getting ready for, what they were planning. They have already brought the housing industry to a halt. We are not building enough homes for the people who need them and they will have to switch to rentals. If we gradually switch enough people to a position where the minority own their own homes and the majority rent, then the imputed rent becomes a feasible prospect for the federal government. That is when they intend to bring it in.

speechtext: Surely you are not serious. You don't believe that.
Yes, he believes it.

The budget was a disaster. The economic strategy of this government is a disaster. If one can believe Maclean's magazine and some of the things said in it about this government, some of the cabinet ministers do not believe this budget will help the economy.

That is right.

May 7, 1982

So why are they not prepared to stand up? It is very easy, if one looks at what happened here a couple of months ago. A number of Liberal members stood up in the House and said we should not have to cut back VIA Rail.
That's right.

They stood in the House and implored the minister not to cut back VIA Rail-and that evening they voted for it. They voted for the cutbacks. That is why you will not see the cabinet ministers voting against the budget or speaking out against the budget, because they do not dare. And why do they not dare? Mr. Speaker, it is because $1 billion per year is spent by this government on political favours, on Liberal Party workers. I said that three times in this House, Mr. Speaker, over the last six months and it has not been refuted yet. No one can refute it.
Inflation in Canada is running at 11.6 per cent, unemployment at 9 per cent. The Conference Board said last week that business executives are slashing inventory, because of cripplingly high interest rates. They go on to report on the Chamber of Commerce that 62 per cent of the chamber's members' venture capital is being invested outside Canada. Why? Because they do not have confidence in Canada; they cannot make a decent return in Canada and they cannot get any support from this government.
That is right.

This government is anti-investment. It is a socialistic government and its policies have been going on for 10 years. It became very clear, when I went to Saskatchewan during the election, that the socialistic policies of this government were not accepted by the people of Saskatchewan. That is why they turfed out the NDP and that is why at the next election they will turf out the Liberals.
It is the divine right of the people.

I hear comments from both sides of the House, Mr. Speaker, from the Liberals and the NDP. They have an unholy alliance where the NDP will support the Liberals as long as the Liberals are promoting socialistic policies. But the NDP is the party that put them back in power. The NDP is the party that supports them. The NDP is the party that is for state ownership.
It is a common-law marriage.
The NDP is the party that tears down, that levels, that makes everybody equal. It is the termite party of Canada.
Oh, oh!

If we look further at the budget, Mr. Speaker, we find a very interesting point. In the budget, the minister of Finance mentioned what he called a typical life insurance policy in Canada, and he used his figures to justify taxing life insurance policies, accrued income every three years. Suddenly
we find out that his figures are wrong. He will not admit it publicly, but they are wrong. He admits privately to the life insurance industry that he was using the wrong figures, but you will not hear him say it publicly. It is an actual fact that the figures he used to calculate the gains on life insurance were based on a wrong policy. He used a non-participating policy. He said he was using figures from the average, typical life insurance policy across Canada. We discovered, and he admits it, that he was using a non-participating policy which only 5 per cent of the people actually buy in Canada. Some 95 per cent of the policies are participating policies. His figures are all wrong but he is not prepared to admit that publicly.
A non-participatory democracy.

We must ask the question, Mr. Speaker, what else is wrong with that budget? What else is wrong with the economic strategy of this government? I thought, Mr. Speaker, that I may have just coined a new phrase, a new word.
The word termites is okay.

Mr. Speaker, looking at the budget we find the government has abandoned the Small Business Development Bond. The banks are not lending money to small business any more under the auspices of the small business development bond. It does not exist. Why would a bank lend money to a business that is failing? That is the only type of business they can lend money to now. Why would they lend any money to it? It is quite obvious that they cannot and they will not, but the Minister of Finance will not admit it in the House. More and more small businesses are going bankrupt each day. They tell me they are spending 20 per cent of their time filling out government forms. They say that the most serious problems facing them in small business are lack of finance, inflation, shortage of skilled help, government regulation and taxation. This government will not rest until all the small business people of the country go bankrupt.
It was very unusual to find the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) in the House today. I have to ask the question, why was he here today when he was in the House talking about the same subject yesterday? It is because he is backtracking on his policies. He was down in Houston telling the American oil industry to come up to Canada to invest. Suddenly he has changed his mind. He knows there is not self-sufficiency in Canada and is therefore trying to bring capital back into Canada. It will not come back. Investors would have to be crazy to come back here. The minister has been discouraging them. That is a major problem.
I see my time is drawing nigh, so I will conclude right now. This government has no direction. The economy is on hold until the next budget in October or November. It is on hold because the government will not backtrack. It is afraid to
May 7, 1982

backtrack because that would harm the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. These are hard times. They are Grit times. Hard times will stay with us until the next election.

Mr. Speaker, I always enjoy the speeches of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Wright). 1 would like to comment on one small portion of his speech just to set the record straight. He referred to who supports whom. This is always interesting because words are rather empty. I know it is quite easy to say where relationships exist and so forth, but the bottom line is voting patterns. The bottom line is who votes with whom. The record shows that over the last number of months the Progressive Conservative Party have voted with the Liberals 29 times. That is all right. As opposition parties we have to vote with the government sometimes when we feel legislation is appropriate, and against the government at other times. However, I want to emphasize the point that the Progressive Conservatives voted with the Liberals 29 times. How many times did the NDP vote with the Liberals? It was not 29 times but just 14 times. I am not a mathematician, but that tells me that the Progressive Conservatives and the Liberals vote together twice as often as the NDP votes with the Liberal Party.
I just put that on the record for clarification. I know the hon. member for Calgary North did not intend to confuse the public, but the record is 29 versus 14. That is enough of that.
I want to thank the Progressive Conservative Party for this opportunity to rise this afternoon and discuss what have been some very critical issues in this country. Those issues are unemployment, the national energy policy, inflation and high interest rates. It is interesting to note that whenever a day is set aside to discuss the most critical issues facing Canadians, the day is never set aside by hon. members opposite. Such debates are never initiated by government members. They are the culprits. It is interesting that the opposition parties take the initiative to initiate debates on isssues which are really important to Canadians.
This morning we received the latest unemployment statistics. I am certain there were many Canadians who were thoroughly disgusted with the response which followed later on in the day. We must all agree that ours is the most prosperous nation in the entire world. Out of 167 sovereign nations, there is no question that Canada is the most prosperous of them all, yet today 1,987,000 Canadians are out of work.
What makes that even worse is that this is the time of year when people generally feel hopeful and optimistic. It is springtime when jobs and opportunities are created. This is the growth period of the year, biologically and chemically, but not in 1982. Over the last month not only were no more jobs created and no more job opportunities opened up, but we also lost 75,000 jobs over the last 31 days. For every 371 people unemployed in Canada there is one job on the board at the employment office.
This is the time when growth should be occurring, but growth is not occurring. There is decay in this country. Opportunities are minimal. What makes that even worse is the
Supply
recognition that hundreds of thousands of young people cannot find work. These are young Canadians graduating from high schools across the country in large and small communities and in rural areas. Tens of thousands of college graduates have skills they have trained for months and, in some cases, years to acquire. University graduates with three to seven years of education behind them are now entering the job market for the first time to meet the challenges of employment opportunities. For most of those people the challenges will not be the challenges of new employment but the challenges of unemployment. Over the next couple of months we will see the dreams, hopes and aspirations of young Canadians dashed, and that is sad. That is why this morning people were disgusted when they viewed the activities of the government. At this time of crisis there is inaction, and the government is not able to come up with new, refreshing and innovative ideas.
What do the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) say? They say there will be more of the same. They say we have to wait and that we cannot do anything. Other countries are doing something. Other countries are taking action independent from action taken in the United States.
There is no question that the relationship between Canada and the United States is very strong indeed and that what happens in the United States will have profound influences on what happens in Canada, but there are independent actions which could be taken. We could be assisting in municipal infrastructure development. We could stimulate the construction and housing industry of Canada. That would instantly put tens of thousands of people back to work.
Of course, we could take a number of other major steps. We could have an industrial strategy which would make sense for the 1980s and would not be dependent totally upon megaprojects, especially megaprojects in the energy field such as those we have seen collapse in the last little while.
What the Progressive Conservative leader said in Montreal the other day was interesting. He was asked for his alternative policy to the present high interest monetary policy. He said he had no alternative. In fact, I think it is well known that the Progressive Conservative Party is looking south of the line and hoping Mr. Reagan is successful with his monetary policy. His policy is the trickle-down policy: give a dollar to the rich, and perhaps a penny or two will eventually trickle down to the regular folks in society. The price Americans are paying today is ten million unemployed. However, I think it was a very honest and respectable gesture when the leader of the Progressive Conservatives said he did not at this point have a policy to offer as an alternative and that he would indeed support Governor Bouey and his monetary policy. I give the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) credit for being honest.
That is not what he said.

I have listened with interest to the speeches of the last number of days. Countless Tories have risen and told of how discouraged they are regarding the role of government in

May 7, 1982
Supply
the economy. They say the real problem is government intervention in the economy and the role government plays in the economy. What do the Progressive Conservatives think about hospitals, schools, universities, colleges, roads, airports, medicare and pensions? They are against government intervention. They say we should let free enterprise do everything. 1 say that is a simplistic approach, but I am not criticizing the Tories; I do not think they mean what they say.
I give them credit, in spite of some of the verbiage and rhetoric we have heard here over the last few days, because I suspect my Tory colleagues would in fact support the Farm Credit Corporation and government intervention in support of agriculture. I know my Progressive Conservative colleagues would support the prairie farm rehabilitation program. I know they would support the land commission act of British Columbia and the farm income insurance program of British Columbia. Why do the Tories say what they say? Why do they react so negatively to the idea that there is some role for the government to play in society?
1 remember my history. I remember the government that introduced the CNR. I remember the government that introduced the CBC. I know what government took over Pacific Western Airlines in the west. They were all Progressive Conservative governments. Why, then, have the Tories reacted so negatively to the role government played in society and in the economy? I suspect it is because of the demonstration of government involvement by the Liberal government and the fact that it has made such an abysmal effort at involving itself in the economy. That intervention is really another form of political expediency.
The hon. member for Calgary North said that $1 billion is spent by the Liberal Party on pork-barreling and patronage. I do not know if that figure is correct but I would not be surprised.
1 have read books that criticized the DREE program because it has provided so much money to support economic activities in areas of the country where there has been no hope of recovery or of economic development following in any realistic way. Why is the money spent in a hopeless area in a hopeless way? If one were cynical one would say it is spent because it buys electoral support, but I would not want to accuse the government of that.
Government support has failed in so many ways. I identify the Candu system and the millions of dollars that have gone into the program but have not brought about any significant return and never will. Yet we see the same program being shored up today. We know the record in Consolidated Computer. There was support for Chrysler Corporation which everyone in this room knew, if they were honest, was a dying corporation. It needed to make dramatic changes but did not respond so the government rushed in with support for an ailing industry. Of course, the support was a guarantee given to an ailing corporation and that is why government intervention has such a bad name.
I do not think anyone is against the idea of supporting ports, railways, airports, medicare and the like. I think of Mr. Lougheed's involvement with Pacific Western Airlines for the benefit of western Canadians. That was probably a good move. I think of the Tory support of Canadian National. That was probably a good move. In Saskatchewan there was support for the potash industry, the telecommunications industry and Saskoil. These were positive moves.
What is the point of your speech?

The point of my speech, for the hon. member who wails at me, is to indicate that there is a role for government in the economy, as is demonstrated by the premier of the province from which he hails.
One of the areas of the world that has often been held up during these difficult economic times as providing the necessary leadership to enable it to carry on with economic growth while others cannot is Japan. There are a variety of aspects of the Canadian economy that one could applaud but I want to focus on total job security for the workers. The Japanese worker has lifetime employment with his employer. This is not the case in Canada where there are nearly two million people unemployed and there is the threat of unemployment for so many more. What does that situation do to create confidence and hope in the future for Canadian workers and investors?
The fundamental problem of our economy is structural. This is the area where the Conservative Party policy puzzles me. I don't think there is anyone who would suggest it is a good idea to have major economic decisions about our future made in foreign countries. Why do we not have more research and development in this country, Mr. Speaker? That is because it is a branch plant economy. Why are more important decisions regarding our domestic future not made in this country? It is because of the branch plant economy. Why is a vigorous effort not made to open up new trading opportunities? That, too, is because we have a branch plant economy.
Statistics Canada estimates that in 1974 the mining and manufacturing industries accounted for 42 per cent of employment and 49 per cent of production. Since then their share of production has been rising constantly but their share of employment has dropped. Of course, it drops in the branch plants. Do the lay-offs that occur in this country occur in the branch plants first or in the parent company? They occur in the branch plant.
This is where my colleagues to my right puzzle me because every day they are asking that FIRA be opened up to make foreign intervention easier, to make it easier for foreign companies to come here as sort of saviours. We have seen what that has done to us in the past and we see what it will do in the future. They want to open up the flood gates and let the foreign entrepreneurs come in. I say that is wrong and it is part of the problem we have today.
I realize that my colleague across the aisle would like to wrap up this opposition day debate and I shall finish early in that case.
May 7, 1982

I have a point of order, Mr. Speaker, which will be brief. This morning members of local 1064 of the United Steelworkers of America ratified their contract with the Sydney Steel Corporation, thus theoretically putting back to work or saving the employment of some 2,400 Canadians. About an hour later the management of SYSCO advised the Nova Scotia government that the lay-offs would be total in terms of production effective Monday morning, meaning that 1,500 or 1,700 of those men will not go to work. Talks have been going on today.
I wanted to express to the chamber that by Monday or Tuesday both the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) will be in a position to respond favourably to the early extention of a rail order from Canadian National for some 88,000 tonnes of steel. I wish the chamber would join the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Transport and the government of Nova Scotia in bringing that about.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say to the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) that I shall make sure that his comments are brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). I think all of us are concerned about this situation and he has offered a practical solution. I am not in a position to say whether such an alternative could be brought about but I shall see that the minister hears the hon. member's comments.
It seems to me that the news we have had today about unemployment is tragic indeed. As a relatively new Member of Parliament I am convinced that any issue involving unemployment is one of the most difficult that any member faces.
We constantly hear from people asking us whether there is some magic spot where the Minister of Finance or the cabinet would draw a line and say: "That is enough unemployment; we will not tolerate it any more and we are going to change our policies". I would have to answer that by saying for most of us, certainly on this side, that the first unemployed person is one too many. I know, whether it be in our constituency offices or through an announcement like the one we just heard from the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East, that it is a horrible feeling for all of us when we cannot respond with immediate help for a man's family and home. But the real issue, the real answer to that concern, comes when we ask ourselves if we can find a genuine and permanent way for our country to grow. The answer is yes, simply because we have the tools to work with. We have the resources, the people, the money and the ideas.
We should not lose sight of the fact that this country has every reason to be optimistic and stop worrying, as one of my constituents did today, over whether we will ever recover. That kind of doom and gloom becomes a self-defeating psychology.
Supply
We have to remember that with the right foundation we can begin our recovery and make it a permanent one. We need to let our markets, our business and our labour force regain their strength. We have to make sure we have a bigger pie, a more productive economy, so that we can take bigger rewards from it. That is the simple message the world and our own circumstances are giving us today.
Let me give just one example. I believe the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) has taken the right course by asking for ways to change the Crow rate. By doing this he has attacked an age-old sickness in our railroads and he is making them stronger, more productive, and more likely to produce jobs and rewards for Canadians in the future.
And more bankruptcies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: We are going to see, as many people from the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona's own province told me a week ago, that decision produce jobs not only for grain farmers and the related industries, but also for people involved with iron ore, coal, potash and all the other resources which have to be shipped from the west to Canadian and foreign markets.
What about the grain markets?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
When we talk about rebuilding our economy we have to address those kinds of tough questions. Just as it is terrible to address the problems of unemployment, so too we must address the problems of structural weakness in our system.
The hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) keeps challenging us to do that on one very good issue, that of foreign ownership. I personally welcome the pressure he puts on in that direction, but he also has to recognize there are other structural weaknesses in our economy. That is the kind of thing we are trying to attack. I do believe we will be ready when our foreign customers are ready as well.
We have heard this afternoon about the terrible unemployment and the slowdown in the B.C. lumber industry. Well, when the American economy rebuilds, that industry will be in a position to respond. But it will do us no good to try and stimulate that industry before the American housing industry is ready to take those products.
Why? Explain that one, Doug.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Because they have no customers for those products.
In Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Instead we need to look at how we can soften the short-term tragedies which occur because of unemployment in the industry. The ministers have been trying to do that through specific targeted programs.
We cannot try to press an industry to grow before foreign customers are ready to accept its products. In my riding, for example, McDonnell Douglas builds passenger aircraft. We

have a marvellous facility and we have seen tragic slowdowns in employment there. In the last two years there has been a reduction in employment from 5,500 to about 2,500 in that one plant. We could solve that problem right away if we placed orders for 20 or 30 DC-10s; but what would we do with them? Equally so, what would we do in many of these other industries where there is some heavy reliance on a weaker external market? Instead we have to take the resources we would use in that fashion and aim them more intelligently to help industry rebuild and guarantee that in the short term the unemployed worker is given full support.
Stimulate the Canadian economy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is why we have stressed inflation as a major problem. It saps our economy's strength and productivity. It pushes up prices and pushes down our ability to compete. It eats up the savings we would otherwise use for investment and makes us uncompetitive. We must improve our position if we expect to keep up with our foreign competitors.
Your policies are worsening inflation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
We cannot abandon vulnerable people or ignore the information we received today from SYSCO or the information we receive from our ridings. That is why we have a series of specific targeted programs, like ILAP in my own riding. The Canadian Admiral Corporation folded, but with the help of ILAP there has been a restoration of over half the jobs immediately, with the promise that several hundred more will be brought back in. In the meantime, the same workers have been given an opportunity for retraining under that program. The UIC moved right in and opened up an office right at the plant to help the workers get their benefits right away. That is how government can respond in a humane and productive fashion.
We see the same thing with the program just announced for Control Data, which is being given a $17 million federal grant to help develop a microcomputer line and software program. Why? Because we are trying to attack the $1.5 billion deficit in computers in our balance of trade. That is targeted program which picks a specific problem and tries to solve it in the short run.
That kind of thinking is reflected in the housing program which the minister responsible for CMHC has developed with
his social housing program. Twenty-five thousand units will be built this year.
Five thousand less than last year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There are 30,000 more units being built under the Canada rental supply program. There is $169 million being spent under the residential rehabilitation assistance program. The Canada home renovation plan is worth another $30 million.
Why are housing starts down?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: We cannot build 200,000 units across the country, but we can stimulate through a targeted program to get as many of those units started as the private sector can afford. That, Mr. Speaker, is the kind of help we can develop in order to attack the short-run problems while the long-term structural problems are sorting themselves out.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. Before I call it five o'clock it has been brought to my attention that comments made by the Chair earlier with respect to a point of order raised by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) may have been out of order in that they constituted an opinion. Just so that members will understand, the hon. member for St. John's East rose on a point of order in reference to the quorum call the other evening. I refused to recognize the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith) for the simple reason that sometimes it does appear to be the duty of the Chair to assist the House in avoiding friction. So it would hardly be consistent if in fact by my intervention I were to add to the friction.
I want to indicate that were it indeed a statement of opinion by the Chair, it was completely inadvertent, and I apologize particularly to the hon. member for St. John's East and to members generally. Obviously it was not my intention to fuel any fires but rather to try and calm them down or put them out.
It being 5 p.m., it is my duty to inform the House that pursuant to Standing Order 58(11) proceedings on the motion have expired. Therefore, the House stands adjourned until Monday at two o'clock p.m., pursuant to Standing Order 2(1).
At 5 p.m. the House adjourned, without question put, pursuant to Standing Order.
